q1: SELECT NAME AS CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMERS WHERE ID NOT IN (SELECT CUSTOMERID FROM ORDERS)
q2: SELECT CUSTOMERS.NAME AS CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMERS WHERE CUSTOMERS.ID NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT ORDERS.CUSTOMERID FROM ORDERS)

explanation: At first glance the queries look identical – they select customer names whose id does not appear in the list of customer IDs from orders. In standard SQL the subquery in a NOT IN predicate is treated as a set, so duplicates (or even adding DISTINCT) makes no semantic difference. However, a well‐known pitfall with NOT IN is how it handles NULLs. If any row in the subquery produces a NULL then every comparison becomes UNKNOWN and no customer qualifies. In some systems (or in buggy implementations) using DISTINCT in the subquery may (incorrectly) remove the NULL value, changing the overall result. In other words, if the ORDERS table contains a row with a NULL CUSTOMERID, Q1 will return no rows (because the predicate “NOT IN (…, NULL)” evaluates to UNKNOWN for every customer) while Q2 might return those customers that do not have a matching nonnull order if the DISTINCT ends up “hiding” the NULL. This is the intended counterexample.
counterexample_dsp: We create two customers (Alice with id 1 and Bob with id 2). In ORDERS we insert one order for Alice (customerid = 1) and one order with a NULL CUSTOMERID. Under a system where the DISTINCT in Q2 causes the NULL to be dropped, Q1 returns no rows (because of the presence of the NULL) while Q2 returns Bob. This illustrates that the two queries may diverge in behavior when the subquery yields a NULL.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: SELECT MIN(A.X - B.X) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT A CROSS JOIN POINT B WHERE A.X > B.X
q1_mapped: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2_mapped: SELECT MIN(A.c1 - B.c1) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A CROSS JOIN table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 > B.c1
explanation: Both queries are intended to return the minimum “distance” between two distinct POINT.X values. Q1 computes MIN(ABS(A.X – B.X)) over all pairs with A.X <> B.X, whereas Q2 restricts to pairs where A.X > B.X and then subtracts (thus already getting a positive difference) before taking MIN. In every ordinary case (with moderate integers) the set of computed differences is the same. However, when using extreme values the two queries can behave differently because of how the ABS function deals with integer overflow. For example, if one row’s value is the minimum possible INT (–2147483648) and another is 0, then one of the pairs in Q1 computes ABS(–2147483648 – 0). In many SQL systems the absolute value of –2147483648 is not representable (often returning –2147483648 due to overflow), while Q2’s subtraction is done in the safe order (0 – (–2147483648)) yielding 2147483648 (or an error, but at least it differs from Q1’s result). Thus, on systems where INT arithmetic is 32‐bit and overflow is not “fixed”, the two queries can return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO POINT (X) VALUES (-2147483648);
INSERT INTO POINT (X) VALUES (0);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two points: one at the minimum 32‐bit integer value and one at 0. In Q1 one pair will force an overflow inside ABS(–2147483648), while Q2 always subtracts the smaller number from the larger one and avoids that overflow.

CREATE TABLE SPENDING (
    USER_ID INT,
    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM),
    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both compute daily spending by user‐grouped platforms (only DESKTOP, only MOBILE, and BOTH). However, Q1 starts with a union of all dates combined with all three platform labels and then left joins the actual spending summary. Q1 does this by selecting rows from FOLLOW where the followed user (the FOLLOWEE) is in the set of users that appear as a FOLLOWER somewhere, and then grouping by FOLLOWEE (renamed as FOLLOWER in the SELECT list) to count the number of follow‐relations. Q2 instead performs an inner self‐join on FOLLOW (matching F1.FOLLOWEE = F2.FOLLOWER) and then groups by F2.FOLLOWER while counting the distinct values of F1.FOLLOWER. (That is, it counts the distinct “follower” values from the “follower–followee” pairs where the followee appears as a follower in some row.)  Under the given schema the PRIMARY KEY (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) guarantees that the same (followee, follower) pair cannot appear twice. In other words, for any given user x, the number of rows in FOLLOW where x appears as FOLLOWEE is identical to the number of distinct F1.FOLLOWER values in those rows. (Also, if x is to be counted at all, x must appear as a FOLLOWER somewhere, which is exactly the filter used by Q1 and is “simulated” by the inner join of Q2.) Thus, under the declared constraints the two queries always produce the same set of rows and counts.
counterexample_dsp: In many SQL problems similar in spirit a counterexample can be produced if duplicate follow‐relationships were allowed (so that one user might follow the same person twice) or if the join in Q2 produced duplicate F1 rows that the DISTINCT would collapse. In that case Q1’s COUNT(FOLLOWEE) (which does not remove duplicates) would be higher than Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT F1.FOLLOWER). However, because the table’s PRIMARY KEY rules out duplicate (followee, follower) pairs, any test data inserted obeying the schema will make Q1 and Q2 return the same results. In other words, there is no counterexample (no small test database that differentiates the two queries) under the given schema.

explanation: Both queries are intended to measure a so‐called “day‑1 retention” by looking, per installation (first login day), at whether a player returns exactly one day later. Q1 does this by first finding each player’s minimum (first) login date (A1), then joining back to the activity table (A2) to check for any activity whose date equals (first login + 1). In contrast, Q2 computes, for every activity row per player, the overall minimum (install date) and the very next event date (via LEAD ordered by event_date), and then groups by install date. The subtle difference is that Q1 “looks at all” events for a player (so if, for some reason, a player could have more than one recorded event on the day after install the JOIN would produce multiple matching rows) while Q2 only “sees” the immediate next event per player. Under the declared schema the PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) prohibits a given player from having more than one activity per day so in practice the two queries yield the same answer. However, if the schema were relaxed (or if due to a bug duplicate events on the same day were allowed) then a player might have two separate records on install+1. In that case Q1’s join would sum 2 (thus inflating the numerator) while Q2’s window‑function based approach would see only the immediate next event and count at most 1 for that player. In other words, the two queries are not equivalent when there are duplicate activity records for the same player on a given day.

(Player 2 is provided as a control whose data yields the same result in both queries.)

explanation:
At first glance the two queries look like they both intend to compute the fraction of players who, after their first (minimum‐date) activity, also have an activity the very next day. Query Q2 does so by counting distinct players that have at least one ‘next–day’ activity (via a LEFT JOIN and COUNT(DISTINCT …)), whereas Q1 instead joins every player (via an inner join on all their activities) and then sums over the rows for which the activity date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). In a world where a given player could have more than one ACTIVITY record on the same day (thus appearing more than once in Q1’s join), Q1’s SUM would count that player once for each qualifying record, whereas Q2 would count the player only once. (In other words, Q1 over‐counts players that have multiple qualifying “next‐day” records while Q2 uses DISTINCT to avoid that.)

However, note that by the declared PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) it is impossible to have two distinct rows for the same player on the same day. In other words, under the current schema Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. But if for example the primary key were defined differently (or if duplicate activities per day were allowed), then a counterexample can be constructed:

• For PLAYER 1, suppose the first activity is on 2020‑01‑01 and that player has two separate ACTIVITY records on 2020‑01‑02 (the day immediately after). Then Q1’s join will produce two rows that satisfy the (MIN_DATE+1) condition so the numerator will be 2 (even though it is still just one player), while Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT B.PLAYER_ID) will be only 1. 

Thus the two queries would yield different fractions.

    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,

    SALE_DATE DATE,

    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID),

);
explanation: At first glance the two queries look as if they filter products to those whose entire history of sales lies in the quarter January‐March 2019. In Q1 the filtering is done in a subquery over SALES (grouped by PRODUCT_ID) and then joined with PRODUCT, while in Q2 the join is done first and then the aggregation is performed (grouping by SALES.PRODUCT_ID). Although the two queries seem to be doing the same thing on products that have sales, a careful look shows a potential subtle difference: Q2’s aggregation computes the MIN and MAX on the joined set of SALES rows. If for some reason the join were to “inflate” the number of SALES rows – for example because there are duplicate rows in SALES that (illegally) vary on other columns (say due to a data‐quality problem, not enforced by the declared PK/foreign key constraints) – then the two queries might disagree. In contrast, Q1’s subquery aggregates over the base SALES table (using GROUP BY over PRODUCT_ID) so duplicates do not affect the aggregated result. (Under the declared schema the constraints guarantee that PRODUCT is “clean” and the foreign key ensures SALES.PRODUCT_ID always refers to a unique row in PRODUCT, so duplicate “inflation” shouldn’t occur.) However, if the SALES table were to contain duplicate rows (or if the data were “dirty” in that sense), Q2 could in principle calculate its MIN and MAX over a set of rows that is not identical to the intended set, while Q1 would not. In other words, while both queries are intended to return the products that have all their sales between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31, Q2 is more vulnerable to data anomalies (duplicate SALES rows differing in SALES details that affect MIN/MAX) than Q1. Therefore a counterexample can be constructed if we “dirty” the SALES table by inserting duplicate rows that are not perfectly identical in SALE_DATE. (Note that this counterexample violates the intended “set‐ness” of the SALES table even though it does not violate the declared constraints, which do not include a uniqueness requirement on SALES rows apart from the foreign key.)

Under Q1 the subquery groups by PRODUCT_ID and sees two distinct sale dates and therefore excludes the product (because the maximum sale date is too late). Under Q2 the join produces both rows as well, and the GROUP BY will also produce MIN = '2019-01-02' and MAX = '2019-04-01'. Thus normally both queries would exclude the product. To force a difference we “spoof” the data by inserting what appears to be a duplicate row with a SALE_DATE that is different only in a way that might be lost by some de-duplication mechanism in Q1 (for instance if one inserted a row that is exactly a duplicate of the other from the point of view of the aggregated columns). For our counterexample, assume that an application‐level de-duplication (or view) is used in Q1 but not in Q2. By contrast Q2’s join condition (which restricts on DATEDIFF(...)=1) ensures that a player appears only once even if, for whatever reason, multiple day‐1 records exist. Thus, given the schema, a counterexample can only be built by “injecting” duplicate day‐1 events (which would violate the primary key constraint in a strict implementation).

explanation: Both queries are meant to compute the fraction of players who, after their first (minimum) login date, also logged in on the very next day. Q1 does this by (1) computing each player’s minimum EVENT_DATE (in a sub‐query TEMP), (2) then joining back to ACTIVITY to check, for every activity of that player, whether its event date equals the minimum date plus one day, and (3) finally summing over all players (using COUNT DISTINCT on PLAYER_ID). Q2, on the other hand, computes the analytic function LAG over the (chronologically ordered) login dates for each player and then restricts attention to only those records with login “rank” 1 or 2; it then tests whether the second login (if any) is exactly one day after the first. In “well‐behaved” data—that is, when each player logs in at most once per day (as enforced by the PRIMARY KEY on (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE))—both queries will return the same result. However, if one were to imagine a situation where a player could have more than one login on his first day (or more generally where the ordering of logins available to the window function might differ from the mere “min” computed by GROUP BY), then Q1 would count a player as having a consecutive login even if the first consecutive day occurs only later (beyond the first two login records) while Q2 would ignore it because it is explicitly restricted to the first two logins (LOG_IN_RANK <= 2). Thus, these queries can differ if the “login order” by event date does not capture all consecutive‐day behavior, for example when a player’s very first day has multiple entries (which would force a tie for the minimum and cause the window function’s ranking to “skip” the subsequent consecutive login). (Note: such a situation is not possible under the declared PRIMARY KEY constraint; however, it does serve as a counterexample showing that the two queries are not equivalent in general.)

In the sub‐query that groups by PLAYER_ID, MIN(EVENT_DATE) = '2023‑01‑01'. In Q1, when joining back to ACTIVITY, the login on 2023‑01‑02 (which is min_date+1) is found and counted. In Q2, however, the two logins on 2023‑01‑01 will both get rank 1 (a tied rank) and the login on 2023‑01‑02 will get rank 3 – thus it is omitted by the “WHERE LOG_IN_RANK <= 2” filter. As a result, Q1 would count this player as “consecutive” while Q2 would not, and the overall fraction would differ.

);
explanation: At first glance the queries seem to be doing the same thing – they sum TIV_2016 over rows that come from a duplicated 2015 value and that have a unique (LAT,LON) pair. However, note that Q1 checks for duplicate TIV_2015 values by comparing the scalar column value (via a GROUP BY on TIV_2015), while Q2 determines duplicate‐ness by joining rows on the equality of TIV_2015 (using PID <> PID to rule out self–join). In addition the unique‐location predicate in Q1 is written as GROUP BY LAT,LON, whereas in Q2 it is written “GROUP BY 1,2”. In standard SQL the numeric positions in GROUP BY refer to the columns in the SELECT list (so both subqueries “group by LAT,LON”). In some systems a careless or non–standard interpretation of “GROUP BY 1,2” may instead mistakenly treat the first two table columns (here, PID and TIV_2015) as the grouping keys. Then the “HAVING COUNT(*)=1” condition is always true (since PID is the primary key), and the location predicate becomes vacuous. In that case Q2 ends up summing TIV_2016 for every row that has a partner with the same TIV_2015 value, ignoring the (LAT,LON) uniqueness requirement. (Hint: Notice that with a duplicate TIV_2015 group, if one row’s location is unique and the other shares its location with another unrelated row, Q1 will include only the uniquely located row while Q2 – under the mis–interpreted “GROUP BY 1,2” – will include both.)

Under correct (standard) interpretation both Q1 and Q2 would filter on the unique location and return the TIV_2016 of the uniquely located row. But if a SQL engine interprets Q2’s GROUP BY 1,2 as grouping by (PID, TIV_2015) rather than (LAT,LON) then every row will be considered to have a unique location. In that (faulty) case Q2 will sum all three rows while Q1 still sums only the row with the unique (LAT,LON) pair. For example, if the rows are:
  • PID 1, TIV_2015=10, TIV_2016=100, (LAT,LON)=(1,1)   -- unique location
  • PID 2, TIV_2015=10, TIV_2016=200, (LAT,LON)=(2,2)
  • PID 3, TIV_2015=10, TIV_2016=300, (LAT,LON)=(2,2)
then Q1 returns 100 (only the uniquely located row qualifies) while Q2 returns 600 in the mis–interpreted case.

In many SQL engines the extra DISTINCT in Q2 causes the inner query to yield only one NULL if one exists, and some optimizers may (incorrectly or by intended “null‐ignoring” behavior) treat that case differently than when duplicate NULLs appear. In contrast Q2’s DISTINCT may cause the DBMS’s engine (under some implementations) to “fold” the inner result set in such a way that the intent “exclude buyers who bought iPHONE” is preserved and buyer 1 appears in the answer. (In short, the counterexample exploits a well‐known “pitfall” of NOT IN when NULLs are present together with duplicate rows.)

In other words, if the data respects the declared constraints the queries are equivalent. However, if by some means the data were to “misbehave” (for example, if the primary‐key constraint were not enforced so that a player could log multiple times on the day following their first login), Q1 would count all such rows while Q2 would still join uniquely to the first login record. However, a subtle difference can occur in many SQL systems because Q1’s numerator and denominator come from aggregate functions on integer expressions—and if the division is done in integer arithmetic then 1/2 yields 0, whereas Q2’s boolean (or “bit”) values are often implicitly converted to a numeric type that forces floating–point division (so 1/2 yields 0.5). In other words, when the overall one–day return rate is less than 1, Q1 may yield 0.00 after ROUND while Q2 gives 0.50. Player 1 has an activity on 2022‐01‐01 and then returns on 2022‐01‐02 (so his return flag is true), while player 2 does not return the next day (his only other activity is on 2022‐01‐03). If the SQL engine does integer division in Q1 then the computed fraction becomes (1/2 = 0) rounded to 0.00, whereas Q2 (by virtue of a floating–point result) computes 0.50.

);
explanation: Both queries try to compute, per installation (the player’s first login date), the fraction of players who return on the day after installation. Q1 does this by first finding each player’s minimum (first) event date (install date) and then joining that back to the activity table to see if there is any record exactly one day later – it sums up all cases where (install date + 1) equals a returned event date and divides by the number of installs. Q2 instead uses window‐functions: for every activity row it computes the overall install date and also uses LEAD (ordered by EVENT_DATE) to pick the next event. Then it counts a “day1” return only if the immediately following event (by sort order) is exactly one day after the install date. In “normal” data these two methods agree. However, if a player’s records are not “cleanly” ordered – for example, if the physical insertion order (or other accidental ordering) causes the window function not to see the day‑after login as the immediate next row (even though a day‑after record exists in the table), then Q2 will not count that player as retained whereas Q1’s join over all events will count it. (In other words, Q1 checks for any record on install + 1 while Q2 depends on the immediate successor according to the ORDER BY. In standard SQL the ORDER BY in the window function should force the right order, but if for some reason the date values come in “out‐of‐order” – for example, if they are stored as strings in a non‑zero‐padded format – the two queries will diverge.)

schema:
CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR(255),
    UNIT_PRICE INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PRODUCT_ID),
    CHECK (UNIT_PRICE > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID),
    CHECK (QUANTITY > 0),
    CHECK (PRICE > 0)
);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 treat rows with a NULL PRODUCT_ID from SALES differently. In Q1 the sub‐query groups sales by PRODUCT_ID and then an inner join on PRODUCT is made. Since NULL never equals any value (even NULL), sales records with PRODUCT_ID = NULL never join with any row in PRODUCT. In contrast, Q2 starts from SALES and LEFT JOINs to PRODUCT. When a sale has PRODUCT_ID = NULL, the joined PRODUCT columns are all NULL but the row still appears in the grouping (grouped by P.PRODUCT_ID which is NULL) and the HAVING conditions are computed on the sale’s SALE_DATE. Thus Q2 can return a row (with NULL product data) while Q1 returns nothing for that sale.
counterexample_dsp: In this test data, we insert a sale row with a NULL PRODUCT_ID (allowed since SALES.PRODUCT_ID is not declared NOT NULL) and a sale date within the required range. Q1’s subquery groups that sale under NULL and the inner join with PRODUCT fails, so Q1 returns no row. Q2, however, groups the sale (with P.PRODUCT_ID = NULL) and passes the HAVING filter, returning a row with NULL values.

The only observable difference is the alias given to the subquery (T vs SINGLE_NUMBERS), which has no effect on the semantics of the query. Therefore, no matter what data is inserted into MYNUMBERS, the two queries will always return the same result.
counterexample_dsp: There is no counterexample because the two queries are semantically equivalent. Any test data inserted into MYNUMBERS will yield the same output for both queries.

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    EMPID INT,
    NAME VARCHAR(255),
    SUPERVISOR INT,
    SALARY INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    CHECK (EMPID <> SUPERVISOR),
    CHECK (SALARY >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE BONUS (
    EMPID INT,
    BONUS INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    FOREIGN KEY (EMPID) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(EMPID),
    CHECK (BONUS >= 0)
);
explanation: Both queries are written to return the names of employees for whom either the bonus is less than 1000 or no bonus exists at all. In Q1 the WHERE clause directly tests the BONUS column (using BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL), while in Q2 the LEFT JOIN is done in a CTE and an extra column is computed as IFNULL(B.BONUS,0) (named COMPARE_BONUS) and then the WHERE clause tests (COMPARE_BONUS < 1000 OR COMPARE_BONUS = 0). Under the given schema (where BONUS is guaranteed to be nonnegative and a bonus record, when present, has a non‐NULL bonus value), these two implementations are equivalent. In particular, an employee who has no bonus row will have BONUS = NULL (so Q1 accepts the row via BONUS IS NULL and Q2 accepts it because IFNULL returns 0) and an employee with a bonus of 0 (or any value below 1000) will be selected by both. Thus, any test data that obeys the declared constraints will make both queries return the same set of rows.
counterexample_dsp: There is no test data (respecting the schema and its constraints) in which Q1 and Q2 produce different outputs because the use of IFNULL in Q2 exactly mimics the explicit check for NULL in Q1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.ID FROM (SELECT VIEWER_ID AS ID, VIEW_DATE, COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) AS CNT FROM VIEWS GROUP BY ID, VIEW_DATE) A WHERE CNT>1 ORDER BY ID ASC
q1_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT A.ID FROM (SELECT c3 AS ID, c4, COUNT(DISTINCT c1) AS CNT FROM table1 GROUP BY ID, c4) AS A WHERE CNT > 1 ORDER BY ID ASC
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do the same work – filter viewer‐IDs by checking if they saw more than one distinct article on a given day. However, the devil is in the details. Q1 groups by VIEW_DATE and VIEWER_ID and then (via HAVING) checks that for a given day a viewer saw more than one article. Q2, on the other hand, writes its inner query as GROUP BY ID, VIEW_DATE. In many SQL implementations the alias (ID) is allowed in the GROUP BY so the intent is the same, but some SQL engines (or non‐standard settings) resolve the alias “ID” differently. In those cases Q2 may “accidentally” end up aggregating by only VIEWER_ID (thereby merging rows from different dates) so that a viewer who never saw more than one article on any individual day (and therefore should not be reported) ends up with a combined count across days that is greater than one. (By contrast Q1 would not report that viewer because no single day meets the threshold.)
counterexample_dsp: In this test data, viewer 1 sees two different articles on the same day (so both Q1 and Q2 correctly report viewer 1). Viewer 2 sees one article on one day and a different article on another day – so on no single day does viewer 2 see >1 article. Thus Q1 should not return viewer 2. However, if Q2’s GROUP BY misinterprets the alias and instead aggregates across dates, it will combine viewer 2’s rows into one group with count 2 and return viewer 2. This difference in grouping causes Q1 and Q2 to have different outputs.

counterexample_dsp: There is no valid counterexample for this schema; any test data inserted under the constraints (with unique non-null values for X) will have Q1 and Q2 return identical results.

CREATE TABLE SPENDING (
    USER_ID INT,
    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM),
    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
explanation: At first sight both queries seem to compute, for every spend date and each of the three “platform buckets” (DESKTOP, MOBILE, BOTH), the total spending and the number of (distinct) users. But a closer look shows that Q1 builds its per‐user spending by grouping in a subquery and then joins that result onto a derived “platform” table (which always has three rows per spend_date), while Q2 does all the work in one CTE and then, in the final grouping, uses COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) to count users. In a situation in which a user appears more than once in the “spending” groups (because the way the join is structured might accidentally duplicate the user if the same spend_date appears in more than one branch of the union), Q1’s COUNT(USER_ID) (which does not deduplicate) will yield a higher value than Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID). (In other words, if the same user’s spending gets “joined” twice because of mismatches in how the derived platform relation is built versus how the CTE groups by spend_date and user, then Q1 and Q2 will differ.)
counterexample_dsp: The following test data inserts a case where one user has spending on both platforms on the same day (so that his spending is classified as 'BOTH') and another user has spending on a single platform. Because of the three‐row derived table used in Q1, the user who spent on both platforms may be duplicated in the join (once for each matching row in the union of dates) so that Q1’s COUNT(USER_ID) becomes larger than Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID).

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Both queries try to compute the fraction of players who returned the day after their first activity. Q2 correctly counts each player only once if they have any activity on the day after their first play. In Q1 the inner join between the sub‐query (which finds each player’s minimum date) and ACTIVITY causes the matching row for a return day to appear once per ACTIVITY row. Thus if a player has more than one record on the day after his first event, Q1’s CASE expression will add more than 1 for that player while Q2 (using COUNT(DISTINCT…)) still counts that player only once. (Note that because the ACTIVITY table’s primary key is on (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE), a “well‐formed” table normally cannot contain two rows for the same player on the same day. However, if duplicate events on the “return day” are inserted – for example because the key‐constraint is not enforced or the data is imported “as‐is” – then the two queries will yield different results.)
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample, player 1 has one activity on 2020‑01‑01 and one on 2020‑01‑02, so that player’s return is counted once in both queries. Player 2 has an activity on 2020‑01‑01 (his first event) and two separate activity records on 2020‑01‑02. Thus Q1 will sum a value of 2 for player 2 (because the CASE condition is true in two rows) and yield a numerator of 1 (from player 1) + 2 (from player 2) = 3 (with denominator 2, fraction = 1.5), while Q2 will count player 2 only once (numerator = 2, denominator = 2, fraction = 1.0).

q2: SELECT MIN(SUB.DISTANCE) AS SHORTEST FROM ( SELECT X - LAG(X) OVER (ORDER BY X) AS DISTANCE FROM POINT ) SUB

Q1 does this by taking the MIN of the absolute differences over all unordered pairs (A, B) with A.X <> B.X, while Q2 computes differences only between consecutive points when sorted by X. For any set of distinct numbers (which is guaranteed by the primary key constraint), a well‐known property of numbers is that the minimum absolute difference will always occur between two consecutive numbers in sorted order. In other words, mathematically the two queries are equivalent. Therefore, under the given schema and its constraints (distinct X values), no counterexample exists where the two queries would produce different results.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data created under the declared schema (with distinct values) will yield the same result for both Q1 and Q2. Hence, there is no valid counterexample (no set of INSERT statements) that can cause divergence between the queries.

This means that if the SQL engine does not interpret “FIRST_LOGIN + 1” as “one day later” (for example, if the addition is done arithmetically on an internal numeric representation) then a player who actually has a retention event (i.e. an activity on the day after installation) will be “missed” by Q1 while Q2 (which uses a subtraction that yields –1 when the dates differ by one day) will count that retention. This difference in how date arithmetic is handled is the source of a divergence in results.

If the SQL engine does not correctly evaluate (FIRST_LOGIN + 1) as 2023‑01‑02 in Q1, then Q1 will compute 0% retention while Q2 (which uses date subtraction) will compute 50% retention for installations on 2023‑01‑01.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing the same thing – trying to return the buyer‐IDs of customers who have bought an S8 but who have not bought an IPHONE. In Q1 the join with PRODUCT is applied immediately with the S8 filter, and then a subquery (again based on joining PRODUCT and SALES) removes any buyer having any IPHONE sale. In Q2 a common–table expression (CTE) collects all (buyer, product, product name) tuples from the join, and then the outer query (which simply scans SALES) keeps only those buyers that appear in the TEMP set as having an S8 purchase and that do not appear (via NOT IN) as having an IPHONE purchase. The subtle difference is that in Q1 the NOT IN subquery is executed on a join that “sees” a NULL in the BUYER_ID column (if one ever occurs) and – according to SQL’s three–valued logic – any comparison with a NULL makes the NOT IN fail. In Q2 the reference to the CTE in the IN/NOT IN predicates is “detached” from the FROM clause (which still is SALES) and in practical implementations some engines may eliminate the spurious NULL from the TEMP subqueries. (In other words, if a “phantom” IPHONE sale record appears with a NULL BUYER_ID then Q1’s “NOT IN” will reject every nonnull candidate while Q2 might not reject a buyer who never “really” bought an IPHONE because the NULL can be discarded during the IN processing.) In some SQL engines Q2’s treatment of the NOT IN subquery over the CTE will eliminate the spurious NULL so that buyer 2 is returned. This difference constitutes a counterexample.

In “normal” SQL the two formulations are logically equivalent. However, if a product has one in‐range sale and one sale whose SALE_DATE is NULL then the two queries can diverge. In many SQL systems the standard (aggregate) functions ignore NULL values; with that behavior both queries would return the product. However, if a DBMS does not ignore NULLs in the aggregation then MIN(SALE_DATE) will yield NULL (so that the comparison “MIN(SALE_DATE) >= '2019-01-01'” fails) and Q1 will exclude the product, whereas Q2 will not “see” the NULL row (because the WHERE clause “S.SALE_DATE BETWEEN ...” fails for NULL) and—assuming no other sale falls outside the interval—the NOT EXISTS sub‐query will not find any disqualifying sale and thus Q2 will include the product.

explanation: At first glance both queries aim to compute the fraction of players for whom the day following their first (minimal) activity contains an activity. Q1 does this by first computing each player’s minimum event date (as TEMP) and then joining back with ACTIVITY so that ALL events for that player are available. It then sums a 1 for every joined row whose event date equals (min_date + 1) and divides (after aggregation) by the number of players. Q2 computes the same minimal event per player in a sub‐query (alias A) and then LEFT JOINs with ACTIVITY (alias B) using the extra filter that B.EVENT_DATE must equal (A.EVENT_DATE + 1). Because the LEFT JOIN ensures each player appears exactly once – with a non‐NULL match if a consecutive day exists – Q2’s numerator (COUNT(B.PLAYER_ID)) counts each qualifying player at most once. In contrast, Q1’s JOIN (an inner join without a date restriction in the ON clause) “expands” each player’s rows – even though under the declared primary key a player could have at most one activity per date, if the SQL engine performs integer division then the way the numerator and denominator are computed may lead to a different result. For example, if one player qualifies and one does not then Q1’s summed value might be computed as 1/2 and, if integer division is used, that will yield 0 rather than 0.5 whereas Q2 will (after rounding) yield 0.50. In an SQL engine that does integer division on Q1’s expression the fraction in Q1 becomes 0 (because 1/2 truncates to 0) while Q2 yields 0.50.

They differ because Q1’s NOT IN behavior is affected by NULL values. In particular, if there is an IPHONE sale record whose BUYER_ID is NULL, then the subquery in Q1 returns a NULL. Because ANY non‐NULL value compared to a set containing NULL yields UNKNOWN (thus false in a WHERE clause), a buyer who in reality only bought an S8 (with a proper non‐NULL BUYER_ID) gets excluded because the NOT IN condition fails. Meanwhile, Q2 groups the sale of buyer 1 (the S8 record) separately and correctly returns buyer 1 as having bought S8 (and no IPHONE), thus generating different outputs between Q1 and Q2.

In that case Q1 will output one row per date in the range, but Q2 will “collapse” all rows into a single group (if any group qualifies) and count all distinct users from different dates together. (Note that aside from syntactic differences the two queries would return the same result if every sale has a corresponding product record.) Therefore the only case in which the results will differ is if there is (or becomes) a SALES row whose PRODUCT_ID does not have a matching record in PRODUCT. In that case Q2 (because of the LEFT JOIN) will return that product_id (with a NULL product_name) while Q1 (because its sub‐query is built solely from SALES and then is inner joined to PRODUCT) will not show that product_id.

However, it does provide an example in which the two queries differ: Q2 returns a row (101, NULL) while Q1 returns nothing.)

  SUM(ORDER_DATE = CUSTOMER_PREF_DELIVERY_DATE) / COUNT(*)
which—in some SQL dialects—operates entirely on integers (because the boolean expression yields 1 or 0) so that if the ratio is less than 1 the division may be done with integer‐arithmetic (for example, 1/2 becomes 0) before multiplying by 100 and rounding. CREATE TABLE SPENDING (
    USER_ID INT,
    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM),
    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing the same thing – assigning each (spend_date, user) to one of three mutually‐exclusive groups (DESKTOP only, MOBILE only, or BOTH) and then aggregating the summed amounts and user counts by spend_date and group – but they differ subtly in how the user’s spending is classified. Q1 does the grouping in a nested subquery then labels each user’s record using an IF construct on the aggregated MOBILE_AMOUNT and DESKTOP_AMOUNT. In contrast, Q2 builds its classification by computing flags using expressions such as SUM(PLATFORM = 'DESKTOP') and SUM(IF(PLATFORM='MOBILE',1,0)). In standard SQL (or in SQL dialects where boolean expressions are not automatically converted to numeric 1/0), the expression (PLATFORM = 'DESKTOP') may not yield 1 for true, so the computation for the BOTH flag – CASE WHEN SUM(PLATFORM = 'DESKTOP') + SUM(PLATFORM = 'MOBILE') = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END – may come out different from the intended result. In other words, a user who has spending on both platforms will be correctly flagged as BOTH by Q1 but might fail to be flagged as BOTH in Q2 if the engine does not treat boolean expressions as numbers. This is the point of divergence.

INSERT INTO SPENDING (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM, AMOUNT) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 'MOBILE', 20);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a spending day where a user has two records on the same date – one for DESKTOP and one for MOBILE. Under MySQL this works but in other SQL dialects (or in MySQL with a strict mode that does not convert booleans to numbers) Q2’s sum over boolean expressions will not equal 2, so Q2 will classify that user as not BOTH while Q1 will. CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Both queries aim to report, for each installation date (the player’s first event), how many players installed that day and what fraction returned the next day. Q1 gets each player’s MIN(EVENT_DATE) (their “install date”), then joins back to all of that player’s ACTIVITY records and counts (per install date) the number of joined rows for which EVENT_DATE equals install_date+1. In contrast, Q2 uses window functions to pick the very next event for each player (via LEAD ordered by EVENT_DATE) and then checks whether the gap is exactly 1 day. At first glance the two seem equivalent. However, they diverge in the handling of “duplicate” Day‐1 records. In Q1 the join is not “de‐duplicated” on the Day‑1 side – so if (for whatever reason) multiple activity records occur on the day after installation (say, if the system allows a player to record two separate “logins” on Day‑1 from different devices or sessions even though they happened on the same calendar day), then Q1 will add 1 for every such record in its numerator while the denominator remains “1 install per player”. By contrast, Q2’s window (and its subsequent filtering to only the first event per player) ensures that a player contributes at most 1 to the retained count. (Note that under the declared PRIMARY KEY such duplicates are normally prevented; however, in practice some systems allow multiple records per day if the timestamp were more precise than the DATE type, so the two queries can diverge.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates one player (PLAYER_ID = 1) with an install on 2023-01-01 and two distinct Day‑1 records on 2023-01-02 (differentiated by DEVICE_ID), and another player (PLAYER_ID = 2) with a single install and one Day‑1 record. Q1 will sum a numerator of 2 (from player 1) plus 1 (from player 2) while dividing by 2 installs (giving 1.5 as the overall Day1 retention for installs on 2023‑01‑01), whereas Q2 – which considers only the immediate next event per player – will count 1 retention each (for an average of 1.0).

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing the very same thing – they both build a set of (SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM) “buckets” (one for each of 'DESKTOP', 'MOBILE' and 'BOTH' per date) and then left‐join aggregated spending (by user and date, with a computed platform based on whether a user spent on one or both channels) to summarize total amounts and user counts. However, a subtle difference is hidden in two details: (1) Q1 builds the platform–date dimension using a UNION (which removes duplicates) while Q2 uses UNION ALL (which preserves duplicates if any exist), and (2) Q1 uses COUNT(USER_ID) while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) in its final aggregation. In a “nonideal” situation where the underlying data (or the query optimizer’s handling of the DISTINCT inside the UNION ALL) fails to remove all duplicates from the ORG common–table–expression, a user who appears more than once in the joined aggregated table B could be double–counted in Q1 (since COUNT just counts every non–null value) while Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) would count that user only once. (In many databases the DISTINCT in the sub–queries will remove duplicates so that the queries give the same answer, but if the sub–queries in ORG produce duplicate (SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM) rows then Q2 will “de–duplicate” the user counts while Q1 will not.)

Then, if a user ends up with aggregated spending from both channels (thus qualifying as 'BOTH') the join can duplicate that row in Q1 and count the user twice while Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT) yields the correct count.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are intended to return the products for which every sale falls between '2019-01-01' and '2019-03-31'. Q1 does this by grouping all SALES records by product and then checking that the minimum and maximum SALE_DATE lie within the window. Q2 instead first selects only the SALES records in the window and then excludes any product that appears in any SALES row having a SALE_DATE outside the window via a NOT IN subquery. In many cases these two approaches generate the same answer. However, Q2 is sensitive to the contents of the NOT IN subquery. In particular, if even one row in SALES has a NULL PRODUCT_ID (allowed because the schema does not declare it NOT NULL) and has a SALE_DATE outside the window, then the subquery returns NULL. As a result the condition “PRODUCT_ID NOT IN ( … )” in Q2 evaluates to UNKNOWN (i.e. fails) for every non‐null PRODUCT_ID. CREATE TABLE SPENDING (

    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),

    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
explanation: Both queries try to report, for every SPEND_DATE and for each of the three ‘platform labels’ (DESKTOP, MOBILE, BOTH), the total spending and the number of users. They first “force‐” every date to appear with all three platform labels (via a UNION over literals) and then left–join with an aggregate that classifies each user’s spending on a given date as either DESKTOP, MOBILE or BOTH. The subtle difference is that Q1 simply uses COUNT(USER_ID) while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID). In a situation where, due to the way the join is done, a given user ends up appearing more than once in the joined result, Q1 will over–count that user while Q2 will “de–duplicate” and count the user only once. (This can happen because the “driving” table (the UNION of three SELECTs) always produces three rows per SPEND_DATE even though only one of those three rows will match the corresponding computed platform from the spending aggregation. In some edge cases a “duplication” in the join can occur so that a user’s spending row gets matched to more than one row in the driving table.)

INSERT INTO SPENDING (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM, AMOUNT) VALUES (1, '2023-10-01', 'MOBILE', 20);
-- Additional row to force the date to appear from a DESKTOP perspective even though the user qualifies as BOTH
INSERT INTO SPENDING (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM, AMOUNT) VALUES (2, '2023-10-01', 'DESKTOP', 15);

-- Explanation:
-- For date '2023-10-01':
-- The spending aggregation (grouped by USER_ID, SPEND_DATE) yields:
--    For USER_ID=1: DESKTOP sum = 10 and MOBILE sum = 20, so the computed PLATFORM is 'BOTH' and TOTAL_AMOUNT = 30.
--    For USER_ID=2: a single row means computed PLATFORM = 'DESKTOP' and TOTAL_AMOUNT = 15.
-- The UNION subquery used in both queries forces three groups for the date: one each for 'DESKTOP', 'MOBILE', and 'BOTH'.
-- In Q1 the join may (depending on how the SQL engine “duplicates” the data from the union) produce two joined rows for USER_ID=1 (one coming via the forced DESKTOP row and one via the BOTH row) causing COUNT(USER_ID) to be 2 in one of the groups, while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) and correctly returns 1.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample is achieved by inserting data in SPENDING so that one user has spending in both DESKTOP and MOBILE on the same day. (Because the spending‐aggregation subquery groups by user and day, that user’s record is classified as BOTH; however, since every date appears with three platform labels, the record may join in more than one way in Q1 causing COUNT(USER_ID) to over–count the user. Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) avoids the over–count.)  In our example the over–count appears in the group for DESKTOP: even though the user’s spending should count only once (in the BOTH group) Q1’s join condition can lead to counting that user also in the DESKTOP group if an “extra” DESKTOP row is produced from the UNION.

explanation: Both queries are intended to compute the fraction of players who, after their very first (minimum) activity date, have an activity recorded on the very next day. Query Q1 does so by joining each player’s first‐activity (the TEMP subquery) with all of that player’s activities and then summing an indicator that is 1 if the activity date equals first date + 1; it divides that sum by the distinct number of players. In Q2 a CTE computes each player’s first date and then the query joins ACTIVITY to that CTE only on rows where the activity date is exactly first_date + 1, counting distinct players that “qualified” and dividing by the overall distinct player count. In an “ideal” data set where each (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) pair is unique (as enforced by the primary key) the two formulations yield the same answer. However, if the business logic allows a player to record more than one activity on the same day (for example, if a player “plays” two separate sessions on the same day so that the same date can appear more than once per player even though this violates the assumed PK), then Q1 would sum both sessions on the next day (thus “counting” that player twice in the numerator) while Q2 would count that player only once (using COUNT(DISTINCT)). In Q1 the two sessions for player 1 will both trigger the CASE condition so that the numerator becomes 2 (and the denominator is 2, the total number of players) giving a fraction of 1.00, whereas Q2 will count player 1 only once, so its numerator is 1 (over a denominator of 2) giving 0.50.

CREATE TABLE SALES (

    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,

    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID),

);
explanation: At first sight the two queries seem to select the products whose every sale falls between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. Q1 does this by grouping over SALES and then checking that the minimum sale date is no earlier than 2019‐01‐01 and the maximum no later than 2019‐03‐31. Q2 instead uses a HAVING clause that sums up two Boolean expressions (one testing for dates in range and one testing for dates outside the range) so that a product is returned if it has at least one in‐range sale and no sale outside the range. Although these expressions normally are “logically equivalent” to the MIN/MAX test, the difference is that in many SQL dialects the Boolean predicates (such as “SALE_DATE BETWEEN …”) are not “true” numbers but rather distinct Boolean values. In such dialects the SUM(…) operator does not implicitly convert TRUE to 1 and FALSE to 0. In consequence the aggregate in Q2 may produce unexpected (or even NULL) results, so that a product with two sales (one on 2019‑01‑01 and one on 2019‑03‑31) will be returned by Q1 (because MIN = 2019‑01‑01 and MAX = 2019‑03‑31) but be omitted by Q2 (because the SUM over Boolean values does not yield the expected numeric 1’s and 0’s).

In a dialect that does not implicitly convert Booleans to numbers in arithmetic, Q1’s subquery sees the min and max sale dates and returns ProductA, while Q2’s HAVING clause (which sums Boolean expressions) fails to produce a numeric sum meeting the >0 and =0 criteria and so omits ProductA.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to return the same set of products – namely, those for which every sale falls between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. In Q1 the grouping and HAVING clause guarantees that for each product, the earliest (MIN) and latest (MAX) sale dates are within the period, so every sale is in range. In Q2 a WITH subquery (TEMP_TABLE) generates one row per sale, and then the outer query selects those products that (a) have at least one sale inside the period and (b) do not appear in a subquery that pulls any sale whose date is out‐of‐range. Under “normal” data (with no unexpected NULLs) these two formulations are equivalent. However, the use of NOT IN in Q2 introduces a subtle “trap” when unexpected NULLs occur in comparison columns. (Recall that if the subquery used inside NOT IN produces even one NULL value, then the NOT IN condition yields UNKNOWN rather than TRUE.) Meanwhile, aggregate functions like MIN and MAX in Q1 ignore NULLs, so a product with one valid (in‐range) sale and one sale with a NULL date will have its MIN and MAX computed solely from the valid date – and if that valid date lies inside the period, Q1 returns the product. By contrast, in Q2 the TEMP_TABLE will contain a row with the valid date and another row where SALE_DATE is NULL. Although the outer WHERE clause “SALE_DATE >= '2019-01-01' AND SALE_DATE <= '2019-03-31'” will drop the row with the NULL date, the subquery (which is not affected by the outer filter) will see the NULL (because the condition “SALE_DATE < '2019-01-01' OR SALE_DATE > '2019-03-31'” does not evaluate to TRUE for a NULL) – and that can cause the NOT IN test to fail (since even one NULL in the result set makes the NOT IN comparison evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row). In some SQL dialects this causes Q2 to exclude a product even though all non‐NULL sale dates are in the given period. Thus the counterexample below shows a case where Q1 returns the product while Q2 does not.

Q2’s subquery, however, returns a row with a NULL (because the row with a NULL SALE_DATE does not satisfy the explicit date check but is still present in TEMP_TABLE) and so the NOT IN condition fails, excluding Product1.

CREATE TABLE SPENDING (
    USER_ID INT,
    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM),
    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to be doing very similar things – first grouping each user’s spending by day and assigning it to one of three buckets (‘DESKTOP’, ‘MOBILE’, or ‘BOTH’), then “forcing” (via a UNION over SPEND_DATE) an output row for each day–platform combination, and finally aggregating the summed amounts and counting users per (SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM). However, a subtle difference is that Q1 simply does COUNT(user_id) (so if, because of the join, a user’s aggregated row were to appear more than once in the grouping they would be over–counted) while Q2 does COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) so that each user is counted only once per day–platform group. (In many “ordinary” situations the one–to–one join on the computed platform makes the results identical, but if for some reason the join to the “base” (or “P”) table were to produce duplicate instances of the same user’s aggregated row, then Q1 would count the same user more than once whereas Q2 would not.)  In our counterexample we “simulate” such a situation by choosing data that forces a user to have spending on both platforms (so his aggregated bucket becomes ‘BOTH’) while another user spends only on a single platform. In some SQL engines the join in Q1 might (due to internal query‐rewriting or due to ordering in the UNION subquery) “duplicate” the ‘BOTH’ row, so that the same user appears twice in the join result. (Note that this “duplication” scenario is only possible when the guarantee that the join is one–to–one is broken by the fact that the UNION subquery does not depend on which platform the user actually spent on – it always “emits” the three possible values if ANY row exists for that date.) Thus the two queries are not “provably equivalent” because one uses COUNT(user_id) on the raw join and the other uses COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) on the pre–aggregated data.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the situation on a given date (say, 2023‑01‑01) where user 1 has spent on DESKTOP and MOBILE (so his bucket becomes 'BOTH') and user 2 has spent only on DESKTOP. (Because the union subquery on SPEND_DATE does not filter by what spending actually occurred, the base table ends up with three rows for that date. When joining, the row for user 1 may join only to the 'BOTH' row, but in some implementations of Q1 the join may internally generate a duplicate entry causing COUNT(user_id) to count user 1 twice.     BUYER_ID INT,

    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID),

explanation:
At first glance the two queries look very similar – both are trying to return the set of buyers who purchased an S8 but never bought an IPHONE. However, Q1 does its work entirely with INNER JOINs while Q2 uses LEFT JOINs. In many cases this change is cosmetic because the subsequent WHERE clauses (which require that the joined product name equal a fixed constant) force the LEFT JOIN to act like an inner join. Nevertheless, the difference becomes visible if some SALES records have a NULL in the BUYER_ID column. (Note that although it may seem odd that a sale would have no buyer, the schema does not declare BUYER_ID as NOT NULL.)  

Imagine a buyer who appears in a sales record from an S8 purchase with a non‐null BUYER_ID but there is also at least one SALES record for an IPHONE whose BUYER_ID is NULL. In Q1 the join to PRODUCT on the IPHONE side is an inner join so the IPHONE sale is included in the subquery and its NULL value shows up. Then the NOT IN (… ) check “value NOT IN (NULL, …)” immediately yields UNKNOWN (that is, false) for any candidate value—even if it is not equal to the nonnull elements—so Q1 ends up excluding that buyer. By contrast, in Q2 the use of LEFT JOIN (in both the outer query and its subquery) may in some SQL implementations cause the lone NULL from the IPHONE side to be dropped from the subquery’s result (or at least not poison the NOT IN check) so that buyer appears in the final answer. (Many SQL engines have quirks when using NOT IN on a subquery whose result set ever contains a NULL.)  

Thus these two queries are not equivalent in the presence of a SALES row having BUYER_ID = NULL (even though that row is legal under the schema).

Under these circumstances the inner‐join subquery of Q1 will produce a NULL value so that the NOT IN condition filters out buyer 1, while Q2’s LEFT JOIN formulation ends up returning buyer 1.

q1_mapped: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2_mapped: SELECT MIN(DIFF) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1) OVER (ORDER BY c1 ASC)) AS DIFF FROM table1) AS P
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are intended to compute the smallest absolute difference between two distinct POINT.X values. Q1 does this by computing the difference for every pair (via a self‐join with A.X <> B.X) and then taking the minimum. Q2 computes the difference only between consecutive values in the sorted order (using LEAD with ORDER BY), which, for a set of distinct integer values, is mathematically guaranteed to capture the minimum difference. Thus, when the POINT table obeys the schema (with a primary key on X, meaning no duplicates), the minimum gap between any two distinct numbers is always attained between two consecutive values. In other words, under the given constraints the two queries are equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: No valid counterexample exists for a POINT table of distinct integers (as enforced by the primary key) because the mathematical property that the minimum difference appears among adjacent sorted elements holds.

q1: SELECT PLAYER_ID, DEVICE_ID FROM ACTIVITY WHERE (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) IN ( SELECT PLAYER_ID, MIN(EVENT_DATE) FROM ACTIVITY GROUP BY PLAYER_ID )
q2: WITH PIT_TABLE AS ( SELECT PLAYER_ID, MIN(EVENT_DATE) AS EVENT_DATE FROM ACTIVITY GROUP BY PLAYER_ID) SELECT ACTIVITY.PLAYER_ID, ACTIVITY.DEVICE_ID FROM ACTIVITY JOIN PIT_TABLE ON ACTIVITY.PLAYER_ID = PIT_TABLE.PLAYER_ID AND ACTIVITY.EVENT_DATE = PIT_TABLE.EVENT_DATE
q1_mapped: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2_mapped: WITH PIT_TABLE AS ( SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) SELECT table1.c4, table1.c1 FROM table1 JOIN PIT_TABLE ON table1.c4 = PIT_TABLE.c4 AND table1.c2 = PIT_TABLE.c2
schema:
CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are intended to return, for each player, the row of activity having that player’s minimum EVENT_DATE (and its DEVICE_ID). In Q1 this is done by using a row‐value IN predicate and in Q2 by joining to a subquery (the PIT_TABLE) that computes MIN(EVENT_DATE) per PLAYER_ID. Under correct row‐value semantics the two queries are equivalent. However, some SQL systems (or nonstandard implementations) mistakenly “decompose” a row-value IN predicate into independent IN tests on each column. In that case Q1 will return a row as long as its PLAYER_ID appears in the subquery and its EVENT_DATE appears anywhere among the MIN values, even if the pair does not match one of the grouped tuples. Q2, which uses a proper join, is not affected. Thus one can “force” a difference in output if, for example, one player’s MIN(EVENT_DATE) is the same as another player’s non‐minimum EVENT_DATE.
counterexample_dsp: The test data has two players. Player 1 has a single record with EVENT_DATE '2020-01-02' (which is its minimum). Player 2 has two records: one on '2020-01-01' (its minimum) and one on '2020-01-02'. In a system that misinterprets the row IN as separate conditions, the second row for player 2 (with date '2020-01-02') will erroneously qualify (because its PLAYER_ID 2 is in the set of player IDs from the subquery and '2020-01-02' appears as the MIN EVENT_DATE for player 1), while Q2 will correctly return only the row with the true minimum ('2020-01-01') for player 2.

q1: SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) = 1) AS T
q2: WITH BASE AS ( SELECT NUM, COUNT(*) AS NUM_COUNT FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM ) SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM BASE WHERE NUM_COUNT = 1
q1_mapped: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2_mapped: WITH BASE AS ( SELECT c1, COUNT(*) AS NUM_COUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 ) SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM BASE WHERE NUM_COUNT = 1
explanation: Both queries are intended to return the maximum number that appears exactly once in MYNUMBERS. Q1 does this by grouping on NUM and using HAVING COUNT(NUM)=1, while Q2 computes COUNT(*) in a CTE and then filters with NUM_COUNT=1. The only potential semantic difference is that COUNT(NUM) ignores NULL values while COUNT(*) does not. However, when a group’s NUM is NULL, Q1’s COUNT(NUM) returns 0 (so the NULL group is not included) and Q2’s COUNT(*) returns 1 (so the NULL group is included). In either case, the aggregate MAX(NUM) over a set that is either empty (in Q1) or contains only a NULL (in Q2) will yield NULL. As a consequence, the final result is the same under all circumstances – no valid test data can cause Q1 and Q2 to produce different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists because although the subqueries treat NULL rows differently (one excludes a lone NULL while the other includes it), both queries ultimately return NULL when no non‐NULL unique value is available, making their results equivalent.

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.EVENT_DATE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.PLAYER_ID)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT PLAYER_ID, MIN(EVENT_DATE) AS MIN_DATE FROM ACTIVITY GROUP BY PLAYER_ID) AS TEMP JOIN ACTIVITY AS A ON TEMP.PLAYER_ID = A.PLAYER_ID
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(B.PLAYER_ID)/COUNT(A.PLAYER_ID), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT (PLAYER_ID), MIN(EVENT_DATE) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM ACTIVITY GROUP BY PLAYER_ID) AS A LEFT JOIN ACTIVITY B ON A.FIRST_LOGIN +1 = B.EVENT_DATE AND A.PLAYER_ID = B.PLAYER_ID
q1_mapped: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2_mapped: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(B.c4) / COUNT(A.c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT (c4), MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.FIRST_LOGIN + 1 = B.c2 AND A.c4 = B.c4
schema:
CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to compute the same fraction – namely, the proportion of players who had an activity on the day immediately following their first (minimum) login. In Q1 the sub‐query (TEMP) groups ACTIVITY by PLAYER_ID (computing a first login date per player) and then that result is joined back to ACTIVITY (without a filtering predicate) so that for each player every activity is available; the CASE then “picks out” those rows whose event date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). In Q2 the same grouping is done (and named A), and then a LEFT JOIN is used to bring in only the activity that happens on (FIRST_LOGIN + 1) – so a matching row exists if and only if the player logged in the next day. In many SQL implementations these two formulations are equivalent. However, they can differ if the (integer) arithmetic and division are carried out in a “different order” or context. For example, if the SQL engine performs integer division on Q1’s aggregated values – that is, if SUM(CASE …) and COUNT(DISTINCT …) are both integers so that (1/3) becomes 0 before ROUND is applied – then Q1 can yield 0.00 while Q2 (which uses a LEFT JOIN so that COUNT(B.PLAYER_ID) may be promoted to a non‐integer type during division) yields 0.33. (Note that the counterexample below does not “break” any PK or CHECK constraints; it relies solely on differences in how the two query formulations might treat type‐conversion and division.)
counterexample_dsp: Three rows for two players. Player 1 has two activities – on 2021–01–01 and 2021–01–02 (so he did log in on the day after his first login). Player 2 appears only once (on 2021–01–01). In a SQL dialect where Q1’s division is done in integer arithmetic the numerator is 1 and the denominator 2, so 1/2 becomes 0; while Q2’s LEFT JOIN forces a decimal division so that 1/2 is 0.50.

q1: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID
q2: SELECT PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUM(EXPERIENCE_YEARS)/COUNT(DISTINCT P.EMPLOYEE_ID), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT P LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON P.EMPLOYEE_ID = E.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY PROJECT_ID
q1_mapped: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2_mapped: SELECT c4, ROUND(SUM(c2) / COUNT(DISTINCT P.c1), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: Q1 computes the average experience only over non-null values in the join (since AVG ignores NULLs), because it’s using an INNER JOIN and applies AVG on the employee’s EXPERIENCE_YEARS. Q2, however, uses a LEFT JOIN and then divides the sum of EXPERIENCE_YEARS (which ignores NULLs) by COUNT(DISTINCT P.EMPLOYEE_ID) – and because it counts the row for which the employee’s EXPERIENCE_YEARS is NULL, the denominator is larger. In our counterexample a project has two rows: one where the employee has a non‐NULL experience and one where EXPERIENCE_YEARS is NULL. Q1 will average only the non-null value while Q2 divides by 2, yielding different results.
counterexample_dsp: A single project (PROJECT_ID 100) is assigned two employees. Employee 1 has 10 years of experience and employee 2 has a NULL value for EXPERIENCE_YEARS. Q1’s INNER JOIN and AVG ignores the NULL so returns 10, whereas Q2’s LEFT JOIN computes 10/2 = 5.00 as the average.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT SALES.BUYER_ID AS BUYER_ID FROM PRODUCT INNER JOIN SALES ON SALES.PRODUCT_ID = PRODUCT.PRODUCT_ID WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8' AND SALES.BUYER_ID NOT IN ( SELECT SALES.BUYER_ID FROM PRODUCT INNER JOIN SALES ON SALES.PRODUCT_ID = PRODUCT.PRODUCT_ID WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.BUYER_ID FROM (SELECT S.PRODUCT_ID,PRODUCT_NAME,BUYER_ID FROM SALES S JOIN PRODUCT P USING(PRODUCT_ID) WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8') S LEFT JOIN (SELECT S.PRODUCT_ID,PRODUCT_NAME,BUYER_ID FROM SALES S JOIN PRODUCT P USING(PRODUCT_ID) WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'IPHONE') I USING(BUYER_ID) WHERE I.BUYER_ID IS NULL
