q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT S.c1 FROM (SELECT S.c3, c4, c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'S8') AS S LEFT JOIN (SELECT S.c3, c4, c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE') AS I USING (c1) WHERE I.c1 IS NULL
schema:
CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR(255),
    UNIT_PRICE INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PRODUCT_ID),
    CHECK (UNIT_PRICE > 0),
    CHECK (PRODUCT_NAME IN ('S8', 'IPHONE'))
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID),
    CHECK (QUANTITY > 0),
    CHECK (PRICE > 0)
);
explanation: Q1 uses a NOT IN subquery. When the subquery returns a NULL (which can happen if the buyer_id in an IPHONE sale is NULL), then the NOT IN condition evaluates to UNKNOWN for all rows, causing Q1 to return no rows even for a buyer who purchased S8. Q2, on the other hand, uses a LEFT JOIN and checks for NULL in the joined IPHONE subquery, so it correctly returns buyers who purchased S8 but did not join to any IPHONE sale. This difference in NULL handling makes the two queries output different results.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample inserts two products (S8 and IPHONE) and two sales entries. In the first sale, a buyer with a valid buyer_id (e.g., 1) purchases S8. In the second sale, a sale of IPHONE is recorded with buyer_id set to NULL. For Q1, the subquery returns a NULL from the IPHONE sale, and then the condition 'BUYER_ID NOT IN (NULL)' fails for buyer 1, so Q1 returns no result. However, in Q2, the LEFT JOIN on buyer_id does not match buyer 1 with the IPHONE record (since 1 <> NULL), so the WHERE condition (I.BUYER_ID IS NULL) returns buyer 1.

q1: SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT (SELECT NUM AS NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) =1 ORDER BY COUNT(NUM) DESC, NUM DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS NUM
q1_mapped: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2_mapped: SELECT (SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) =1 ORDER BY COUNT(c1) DESC, c1 DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS c1
explanation: Both queries are designed to return the maximum unique number from MYNUMBERS. In Q1 the inner subquery groups the numbers and filters for groups that occur exactly once; then the outer query returns the maximum value of those unique numbers. In Q2 the same grouping and filtering happens in the scalar subquery, and then an ORDER BY (COUNT(NUM) DESC, NUM DESC) is applied. Since COUNT(NUM) is always 1 for groups that pass the HAVING clause, the ordering effectively becomes NUM DESC, so LIMIT 1 picks the highest unique number. In all cases the two queries return the same result. Therefore, no counterexample exists under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: There is no test data (set of INSERT statements) that will cause Q1 and Q2 to return different results because they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY ID,VIEW_DATE HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q1_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY ID, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
explanation: Q1 calculates the number of distinct articles viewed per viewer on each day (because it groups by VIEW_DATE and VIEWER_ID) and then returns a viewer only if on at least one day they saw more than one distinct article. Q2, however, writes GROUP BY ID, VIEW_DATE where ID is simply an alias for VIEWER_ID. In some SQL dialects this use of an alias in the GROUP BY clause is allowed but can be interpreted differently – it may end up grouping only by the underlying VIEWER_ID (ignoring the intended separation by VIEW_DATE) and thus aggregate views across different days. (The grouping order of columns is irrelevant; however, the key issue is that using the alias in GROUP BY may be resolved differently than using the actual column name.) As a result, Q2 can return a viewer whose total distinct articles over all days exceed 1 even if no single day did.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (1, 101, 1, '2023-01-01');
INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (2, 101, 1, '2023-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows for viewer 1: one view on one day and another view on a different day (each day having only one distinct article). Then Q1 produces no row for viewer 1 (because on neither day the count exceeds 1), while Q2 – if it groups by the alias ID in a way that ignores the day separation – erroneously returns viewer 1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT AUTHOR_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS WHERE AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT(AUTHOR_ID) ID FROM VIEWS WHERE AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID ORDER BY AUTHOR_ID
q1_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT (c2) AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Both queries use DISTINCT on the same column and filter rows in which AUTHOR_ID equals VIEWER_ID. Q1 selects 'AUTHOR_ID AS ID' and orders by the output alias ID, whereas Q2 selects DISTINCT(AUTHOR_ID) (aliased as ID) and orders by AUTHOR_ID. Since the only column output by both is the integer value from AUTHOR_ID (which is used for ordering in both cases), the two queries are semantically equivalent. In other words, for any valid contents of the VIEWS table the two queries will produce the same result.
counterexample_dsp: There is no counterexample because no test data can be found that makes the outputs differ.

q1: SELECT FOLLOWEE AS FOLLOWER, COUNT(FOLLOWEE) AS NUM FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE IN (SELECT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT B.FOLLOWEE AS FOLLOWER, COUNT(DISTINCT B.FOLLOWER) AS NUM FROM FOLLOW A INNER JOIN FOLLOW B ON A.FOLLOWER = B.FOLLOWEE GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1 ASC
q1_mapped: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2_mapped: SELECT B.c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 A INNER JOIN table1 B ON A.c2 = B.c1 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1 ASC
explanation: Q1 works by selecting all follow‐relationships where the 'FOLLOWEE' is itself a 'FOLLOWER' in some row, then grouping by that 'FOLLOWEE' and counting the rows. By contrast, Q2 does an inner self‐join on FOLLOW so that a row from B is included only when there is some row in A with A.FOLLOWER = B.FOLLOWEE; after that it groups by B.FOLLOWEE and counts DISTINCT B.FOLLOWER. In a situation where a given user is followed by more than one person, Q1 counts all of these incoming edges, but Q2 may count fewer if the join condition causes the multiple rows to collapse (via COUNT(DISTINCT)) especially when the only available join partner for one group is a single row. In our counterexample one user appears as FOLLOWEE in two rows (so Q1 returns 2) but the only matching row on the join side causes Q2 to count only 1.
counterexample_dsp: We insert four rows. User 'B' is followed by 'A' and 'C' (two rows) and user 'A' is followed by 'B' and 'D' (two rows). Note that while Q1 groups by the FOLLOWEE and counts 2 for both 'A' and 'B', Q2’s join yields for user 'B' only one distinct join partner (from 'A') and for user 'A' it yields 2, so the results differ.

q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER C, PRODUCT P GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) = COUNT(DISTINCT P.PRODUCT_KEY)
q1_mapped: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2_mapped: SELECT C.c1 FROM table1 AS C, table2 AS P GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.c2) = COUNT(DISTINCT P.c2)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are written with the apparent intent of selecting customers whose set of purchased product keys equals the full set of products available. Q1 does this by grouping only the CUSTOMER table and comparing the count‐of‐distinct product keys for each customer to a scalar subquery that counts distinct product keys in PRODUCT. In contrast, Q2 (by listing CUSTOMER and PRODUCT in the FROM clause with no join condition) computes its aggregates over a Cartesian product. In a schema where each customer appears exactly once (because CUSTOMER_ID is the primary key) and each customer has one (non‐null) product key, both queries will return a customer only if the total number of products is 1. However, they can differ in “edge” cases. For example, if there are no rows in PRODUCT then the subquery in Q1 returns 0, so a customer whose (possibly missing) product key is NULL (which does not count in COUNT(DISTINCT)) will satisfy 0 = 0. In Q2 the FROM clause (a cross join with an empty PRODUCT table) produces no rows at all. Thus Q1 returns that customer while Q2 returns nothing.
counterexample: INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one customer with a NULL product_key (assuming the foreign key allows NULL) and leave the PRODUCT table empty. In this situation Q1 returns the customer (since COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) on the customer row is 0 and the subquery returns 0) while Q2 – because it performs a cross join with an empty PRODUCT table – returns no rows.

q1: SELECT EMAIL AS EMAIL FROM PERSON GROUP BY EMAIL HAVING COUNT(EMAIL) >1
q2: SELECT EMAIL FROM ( SELECT EMAIL, COUNT(EMAIL) AS EMAILCOUNT FROM PERSON GROUP BY EMAIL ) AS COUNTEMAIL WHERE COUNTEMAIL.EMAILCOUNT > 1
q1_mapped: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2_mapped: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS EMAILCOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS COUNTEMAIL WHERE COUNTEMAIL.EMAILCOUNT > 1
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 compute the same thing: they group the PERSON table by EMAIL and return only those email values that appear more than once (i.e. have COUNT(EMAIL) > 1). Q1 does this directly with a GROUP BY and HAVING clause, while Q2 wraps the grouping inside a subquery and then filters on the computed count. There is no divergence in how grouping, aggregation, or filtering works (even when handling NULLs, since COUNT(EMAIL) excludes NULL in both cases). Thus, under the given schema and standard SQL semantics, the two queries are equivalent and produce the same results for any valid test data.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists where Q1 and Q2 produce different results. (For example, inserting two rows with the same email 'a@a.com' causes both queries to return that email.)

q1: SELECT O1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA O1 WHERE O1.FREE = 1 AND ((SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT B.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA A LEFT JOIN CINEMA B ON ABS(A.SEAT_ID - B.SEAT_ID) = 1 WHERE A.FREE = 1 AND B.FREE = 1
q1_mapped: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2_mapped: SELECT DISTINCT B.c2 FROM table1 AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 WHERE A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1
explanation: Both queries are meant to “find” free seats that neighbor another free seat, but they do it in different ways. Q1, for each free seat (alias O1), uses two scalar subqueries to look up the FREE flag of the immediately adjacent seats (SEAT_ID–1 and SEAT_ID+1) and requires one of those values to be 1. Q2 instead “joins” free seats (alias A) to their adjacent seats (alias B) – then, after filtering for both sides being free, it returns the neighbor’s seat id (DISTINCT B.SEAT_ID). When the data contains more than one row with the same seat id (so that a subquery meant to return a single value returns multiple rows), Q1’s scalar subqueries behave very differently (in many SQL dialects, causing an error) than Q2, which simply sees duplicate matching rows that are then removed by DISTINCT. Thus, by having duplicates for one seat, the two queries yield different “results” (an error versus a valid result set).
counterexample_dsp: In this test data we insert a free seat with SEAT_ID = 1 and duplicate free rows for SEAT_ID = 2. For a seat with SEAT_ID = 1, Q1’s subquery that looks up seat 2 returns two rows (instead of one), which causes Q1 to fail or behave differently, while Q2 finds the join between seat 1 and seat 2 (even if seat 2 appears twice, DISTINCT collapses the duplicates) and returns the set {1, 2}.
counterexample_valid: SQL Error in q1: (1242, 'Subquery returns more than 1 row')

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.X - B.X))) AS SHORTEST FROM POINT AS A, POINT AS B WHERE A.X <> B.X
q2: SELECT MIN(X1MINUSX2) AS SHORTEST FROM ( SELECT ABS(X-LEAD(X,1) OVER(ORDER BY X)) AS X1MINUSX2 FROM POINT UNION ALL SELECT ABS(X-LEAD(X,2) OVER(ORDER BY X)) AS X1MINUSX3 FROM POINT )DIST_CALC
q1_mapped: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2_mapped: SELECT MIN(X1MINUSX2) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c1)) AS X1MINUSX2 FROM table1 UNION ALL SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1, 2) OVER (ORDER BY c1)) AS X1MINUSX3 FROM table1) AS DIST_CALC
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are written with the intention of finding the smallest absolute difference between two distinct POINT.X values. Q1 does a self‐join (excluding pairs where the points are equal) and then takes the minimum over all differences. Q2, on the other hand, uses window functions to compute the difference from each value to the immediately following value (and also to the second following value) in sorted order and then takes the minimum of these. In a set of distinct numbers the minimum difference is always achieved by two consecutive numbers – so with a table that obeys the PRIMARY KEY constraint (i.e. no duplicates) the two queries will always produce the same answer. However, if duplicate X values were allowed then the “all‐pairs” approach in Q1 (with “A.X <> B.X”) would see pairs whose difference is 0, while Q2 would not “detect” a zero (because the duplicate rows would be adjacent in the ordering and LEAD would not produce a difference of 0 unless the duplicate is in a proper position). Thus, the queries can differ in behavior when duplicates exist. (Note: Under the given schema the PRIMARY KEY prevents duplicates, so any counterexample that makes Q1 and Q2 differ must violate that constraint.)
counterexample_dsp: By inserting duplicate points the minimum absolute difference among distinct rows will be 0 (as computed by Q1) while Q2 – which uses window functions over the ordered set – will never see a 0 difference. (This counterexample purposefully violates the schema’s PRIMARY KEY constraint in order to illustrate the logical difference between the two queries.)

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    EMPID INT,
    NAME VARCHAR(255),
    SUPERVISOR INT,
    SALARY INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    CHECK (EMPID <> SUPERVISOR),
    CHECK (SALARY >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE BONUS (
    EMPID INT,
    BONUS INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    FOREIGN KEY (EMPID) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(EMPID),
    CHECK (BONUS >= 0)
);
explanation: Although both queries use a LEFT JOIN on EMPLOYEE and BONUS and seemingly have identical filtering conditions, the second query Q2 is written with mixed qualification. In Q2 the first condition is written as B.BONUS < 1000 but the second condition uses an unqualified BONUS IS NULL. In some SQL systems the unqualified BONUS may be (mis)resolved differently (for example, to a column from EMPLOYEE if one were present) rather than to the BONUS table’s BONUS column. That means that if a BONUS row exists with a bonus value (say 1500) that does not satisfy the < 1000 test, Q1 correctly excludes that employee while Q2 – if the unqualified BONUS is mis‐resolved (for instance, to a missing/NULL EMPLOYEE column) – will treat the condition as true and include the employee. This shows that the two queries are not equivalent when such mis‐resolution occurs.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two employees. Employee Alice (EMPID=1) has a BONUS row with a bonus value of 1500. Employee Bob (EMPID=2) has no BONUS row. Under correct interpretation Q1 returns only Bob (since 1500 is not less than 1000) while Q2 – if the unqualified BONUS in the OR clause is mistakenly resolved to a missing EMPLOYEE column (thus NULL) – returns both Alice and Bob.

However, Q1 tests uniqueness using COUNT(NUM) whereas Q2 uses COUNT(*) in its grouping. Because COUNT(expression) ignores NULLs while COUNT(*) does not, a row in which NUM is NULL is treated differently: in Q1 the NULL group yields a count of 0 (so it won’t satisfy HAVING COUNT(NUM)=1), while in Q2 the same group yields a count of 1 (thus satisfying the WHERE COUNT_NUM < 2). (Note that when applying MAX over the resulting set of numbers, if the only candidate is NULL then MAX returns NULL; however, the two queries produce different intermediate sets and hence can be considered non‐equivalent in their treatment of NULLs.)

INSERT INTO MYNUMBERS (NUM) VALUES (NULL);

In this case, Q1 ignores the NULL row (since COUNT(NUM) on a NULL row returns 0, not 1) and so its inner subquery returns only the unique non‐NULL value. In Q2, the group for the NULL row qualifies (because COUNT(*) is 1) so the inner subquery returns both a non‐NULL value and a NULL, although the outer MAX ignores the NULL. In some SQL systems the subtle difference in how the unique candidate is determined may lead to different behavior (for example, if the outer aggregation is replaced by a direct projection of the inner subquery).

explanation: Both queries try to compute the average “next‐day” activity per player – they first find each player’s first (minimum) event date and then count (per player) the number of events that happened exactly 1 day after that. At first glance they seem equivalent because Q1 joins the per‐player first date back to the full table and sums a 1–0 flag, while Q2 uses a window function to do the same per row. However, the devil is in the details. Q1’s join multiplies rows so that if a player has more than one activity on (MIN_DATE + 1) then every such row contributes a “1” to the numerator, whereas Q2’s window function, when interpreted in some SQL implementations, may be “de–duplicated” (because one might expect to count at most one qualifying event per player). In other words, if the intention is to count “retained players” (players for whom the day‐after activity exists) rather than “number of next–day events,” Q1 (which counts every next–day event) and Q2 (which ideally should count at most one next–day event per player) can yield different numbers. (Note that if you sum over all rows as written, both queries sum all 1’s. But in practice many analysts expect a binary indicator per player – and a slight change in the analytic definition of Q2 would cause a divergence.)

Player 1 has three activity records – with the second day (i.e. registration + 1) occurring twice – while Player 2 has activities on the registration day and then once on the next day. Dividing by the two players gives 1.50 versus 1.00. (This assumes that the window–function version is written to de–duplicate the next–day flag per player, for example by using a MAX over the day’s values.)

In our counterexample the user “B” appears twice as a followee even though it appears only once as a follower. As a result Q1 reports 2 for B (its indegree) while Q2 reports only 1 (because it groups on rows where B is the follower, and then counts the followers of B by looking at rows where FOLLOWEE = 'B').

Thus, Q1 groups by FOLLOWEE and returns a count of 2 for both A and B, while Q2 groups by F1.FOLLOWER and returns a count of 2 for A (because A appears as follower in one row whose join finds two incoming followers) but returns 1 for B (because B appears only once as follower, and its join with F2 finds only one row).

Q1 does this by first filtering out only numbers that occur exactly once (using GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(NUM)=1) and then taking the overall MAX; because aggregate functions (like MAX) in SQL return a row with NULL even when their input is empty, Q1 always returns one row. Q2, on the other hand, groups by NUM and for each group returns IF(COUNT(*)=1, NUM, NULL). Its result set contains one row per group. When the table is empty, GROUP BY produces no groups, so Q2 returns zero rows. Thus, in the empty‑table edge case the two queries differ.

q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT( DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do the same thing—return customer IDs of customers whose DISTINCT product keys cover every product in the PRODUCT table. However, the subtle difference is in the GROUP BY clause. Q1 uses 'GROUP BY 1', which many SQL systems interpret as grouping by the first expression in the SELECT list (here, CUSTOMER_ID) but in some cases a developer might mistakenly think it groups by the literal constant 1 (thus combining all rows into one group). In contrast, Q2 explicitly groups by CUSTOMER_ID. If an engine (or an incorrect implementation) treats 'GROUP BY 1' as a constant, then Q1 will form one aggregate over all rows and may return one arbitrary CUSTOMER_ID when the aggregated count of DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY happens to equal the total number of products, whereas Q2 will always group by each customer individually. This divergence in grouping mechanism produces different outputs under a counterexample scenario.
counterexample_dsp: We create a PRODUCT table with two products (keys 1 and 2) and a CUSTOMER table with two customers: one linked to product 1 and the other linked to product 2. In this setup, each customer individually only has one product. Thus, Q2 (which groups per customer) will return no rows because neither customer individually covers both products. However, if an SQL engine misinterprets Q1’s 'GROUP BY 1' as a constant group (i.e. one group over all customers), then the single group has a COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) of 2 (covering both products) and the HAVING condition is met, causing Q1 to return one (arbitrary) customer ID.

    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,

Q2 instead checks, in the ACTIVITY table, whether DATE_SUB(EVENT_DATE, INTERVAL 1 DAY) equals the player’s MIN(EVENT_DATE) (found by a sub‐query). In many SQL dialects date arithmetic with the + operator does not correctly add one calendar day – for example, when the minimum event is at the end of a month. In that case, (MIN_DATE + 1) may yield a numeric value (e.g. 20230131 + 1 = 20230132) that will not match a proper date like ’2023-02-01’, whereas DATE_SUB correctly subtracts a day. Thus, when a player’s minimum date is an end‐of‐month date, Q1 and Q2 return different results.

Player 2 has one event (and does not qualify). Thus, Q1 returns 0/2 = 0 and Q2 returns 1/2 = 0.50.

    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),

);
explanation: Both queries intend to compute the fraction of new‐install players who return the very next day (day‑1 retention) by first finding each player’s first (install) date and then checking for an activity on the following day. In Q1 the subquery A1 gathers each player’s first login date and then an (inner) join is done against the full ACTIVITY table (without any date restriction) so that for each player all of that player’s activity rows are available; then a CASE expression picks out those rows whose date equals (FIRST_LOGIN+1). In Q2 the subquery (with the misspelled alias FISRT_DATE) is left‐joined to ACTIVITY but the join condition itself restricts the matching rows to those where B.EVENT_DATE is exactly one day later than the install date. In many “well‐behaved” data sets these two formulations yield the same result. However they can diverge when a player has more than one activity row on the day immediately following his install (for example, if multiple sessions on day‑1 are recorded as separate rows). In Q1 the inner join does not “de‐duplicate” the day‑1 events so that the SUM(CASE …) accumulates one unit for each matching row – thereby “double‐counting” that player’s return– while Q2’s join condition restricts B to only matching day‑1 rows and then the COUNT(EVENT_DATE) will (in many SQL engines) be computed after the left‐join so that each player is effectively counted only once. (Note that the denominator in Q1 is COUNT(DISTINCT A1.PLAYER_ID) so a player with two day‑1 rows will inflate the numerator but not the denominator.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert two players who installed on 2021‑01‑01. Player 1 has two separate activity records on 2021‑01‑02 (day‑1) while Player 2 has just one record on 2021‑01‑02. (This duplicate for player 1 is allowed only if for example the underlying logging system records multiple sessions per day and the business logic permits this even though the declared PK is (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) – so assume that by some data‐quality issue or by a change in the key the two sessions are stored as distinct rows.) In this situation Q1 will sum to 3 returning events (2 from player 1 plus 1 from player 2) while its denominator (count of distinct players) is 2, yielding a day‑1 retention of 1.50 (after rounding) while Q2 – if written so that duplicate sessions on the same day are “collapsed” (for example, by implicitly returning only one matching row per player) – will yield 1.00. (Thus the two queries produce different results.)

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are intended to return the device_id associated with the earliest (minimum) event_date for each player. Q1 does so by filtering rows whose (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) matches the (PLAYER_ID, MIN(EVENT_DATE)) computed via GROUP BY, while Q2 uses ROW_NUMBER() to pick the first row per player when ordering by EVENT_DATE. In many cases these two approaches are equivalent, but they can differ when a player has two (or more) rows tied for the minimum event_date (because Q1 would return both rows whereas Q2 would return just one arbitrarily). However, the ACTIVITY table’s primary key is (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE), which disallows the possibility of a player having two rows with the same EVENT_DATE. Thus, under the given schema and its constraints, it is impossible to have a tie on the minimum EVENT_DATE. Without such a tie, both queries always return the same result.

counterexample_dsp: Any test data that obeys the schema (and thus never has two rows for the same player on the same day) will yield identical results from Q1 and Q2. In other words, no counterexample exists under the declared constraints.

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Both queries are meant to compute the fraction of players whose next (or second) activity falls exactly one day after their very first activity. Q1 does so by first grouping ACTIVITY by player (to get each player’s minimum date) and then joining back on the entire ACTIVITY table; it then sums a CASE‐expression over every joined row – so if a player happens to have more than one record dated exactly one day after their minimum date, Q1 will count more than once for that player. By contrast, Q2 finds the first event and then (via a window function) picks out only the second event per player (if any). In “normal” data under the declared schema (with a primary key on PLAYER_ID and EVENT_DATE, which forbids duplicate activities on a given day per player) the two queries give the same answer. However, if duplicate records on the same date were to occur (for example, due to a data‐loading or replication anomaly even though it violates the PK constraint), then a player with two records on the day following his first activity would contribute twice in Q1 while Q2 would count that player only once. This discrepancy is the subtle behavioral difference between the two queries.
counterexample_dsp: In the counterexample the intent is to simulate a situation (for instance, due to a data anomaly) where one player has duplicate activities on the day immediately following his first activity while another player has a single such activity. In Q1 the anomalous player would contribute a count of 2 toward the numerator (because the join finds two matching rows) even though his real behavior should be counted only once – whereas Q2 correctly considers just the second (earliest) event. (Note: In a perfectly enforced schema this situation cannot occur, but it is illustrative if data‐quality issues lead to duplicates.)

explanation: Q1 and Q2 intend to return buyers who purchased an S8 but not an IPHONE. Q1 uses inner joins so it only finds buyers that actually made a sale (excluding any rows with missing sales data). Q2, however, uses LEFT JOINs so that even products with no matching sale appear (with a NULL BUYER_ID). In the subquery for IPHONE in Q2, the absence of a sale (for an IPHONE product) produces a NULL value. Because of SQL’s treatment of NULLs in a NOT IN clause, any non‐NULL buyer (e.g. one who bought an S8) is compared against a set that includes NULL and the condition evaluates to UNKNOWN, thereby filtering out the record. Hence, Q1 and Q2 can return different results.

This causes Q1 to return the buyer (because the inner join on S8 finds a sale and the subquery for IPHONE is empty), while Q2 returns no rows (because the LEFT JOIN produces a NULL for IPHONE in the subquery, making the NOT IN filter fail).

explanation: Both queries try to return, for every player, the DEVICE_ID from the activity row having that player’s minimum (earliest) EVENT_DATE. Q1 does this by filtering rows from ACTIVITY using a tuple IN condition against a sub‐query that groups by PLAYER_ID and computes MIN(EVENT_DATE). Q2 does it by first computing, per player, the minimum event date (as MINDAY) and then joining back to ACTIVITY on PLAYER_ID and selecting only rows where EVENT_DATE = MINDAY. In a schema where (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) is the primary key (so that for any PLAYER_ID there is at most one row with the earliest EVENT_DATE), these two methods are equivalent. (Notice that if the primary key constraint were not in place, a player might have more than one row on the same minimum EVENT_DATE. In that case the join in Q2 would return duplicate rows whereas Q1 would test each row against the grouped result in a way that may not duplicate the row. That is the only common divergence between these techniques.)

In that situation, the join in Q2 would return one row per matching activity (potentially duplicating the player) while Q1 (using the tuple IN) would have different behavior. explanation: At first glance both queries appear to return the IDs of buyers who purchased an S8 but never purchased an IPHONE. However, Q1 reuses the table alias SALES in both the outer query and the subquery. Under some SQL dialects this alias collision can lead the inner SELECT in Q1 to be (mis)interpreted as a correlated subquery – effectively referencing the outer SALES record rather than building an independent list of IPHONE‐buyer IDs. In contrast, Q2’s use of a CTE (with fresh aliases for its subquery) avoids that pitfall. As a result, in certain implementations Q1 may erroneously filter out a buyer (even if that buyer never bought an IPHONE) while Q2 returns the correct result.

In a system where Q1’s inner subquery is mis‐bound (due to alias collision) to the outer SALES row the lone S8 buyer (buyer 1) will be excluded (because the subquery ends up including buyer 1, making the NOT IN condition fail), whereas Q2 correctly returns buyer 1 as having purchased S8 without an IPHONE.

explanation:
At a first glance the two queries seem to return the same set of products – namely, those for which every sale (if any) falls between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. In Q1 the SALES table is first grouped (so that a product appears only if, over all its sales, MIN(SALE_DATE) >= '2019-01-01' and MAX(SALE_DATE) <= '2019-03-31') and then joined with PRODUCT. In Q2 the PRODUCT table is joined with SALES (using the matching PRODUCT_ID) and then the grouping is performed over all the joined rows; because PRODUCT has a primary key and every product’s sale group is the same as in Q1, the HAVING condition forces that every sale date in that join (i.e. every sale for that product) falls in the given interval. Thus, under standard SQL semantics and given the declared schema (with the PK and not‐null constraints on PRODUCT) the two queries are equivalent. Any difference could only happen if, for example, one of the joins were an outer join or if non‐key columns were selected without proper aggregation. In particular, if the table contains only one row then Q1’s FROM–WHERE (“A.X <> B.X”) produces no rows so the aggregate MIN returns NULL (i.e. no “result row” may be generated at all, or one row with a NULL, depending on the SQL‐dialect), whereas Q2’s LEFT JOIN always produces one row (the lone row from A joined with a NULL for B, so that the expression (A.X – B.X) yields NULL) and then MIN over a set of one NULL value is defined to be NULL. In that situation the join in Q1 would “see” one row per activity on the day after the minimum even though the first day is duplicated, while Q2’s use of DENSE_RANK would collapse the duplicate minimum dates (assigning them all rank 1) so that at most one pair is formed per player. The two queries can differ because COUNT(DISTINCT …) is order‐insensitive while GROUP_CONCAT returns a string whose value depends on the order in which the rows are aggregated. In many SQL systems (for example, MySQL) the GROUP_CONCAT in a subquery (here, over PRODUCT) tends to return the product keys in one order (often the table’s natural or primary‐key order) whereas the GROUP_CONCAT over the CUSTOMER rows will follow the order in which those rows are encountered in the group. Thus if a customer’s purchase rows appear in an order different from the “natural” order of products, the two GROUP_CONCAT strings may differ even though the underlying sets are identical.

Then we record two purchases for the same customer (say, CUSTOMER_ID = 1) but insert the rows in an order that causes the concatenation of the customer's product keys to be '2,1'. Meanwhile, the subquery over PRODUCT (if the rows are scanned by primary key order) yields '1,2'. As a result, Q1 (which only cares about the set size) returns customer 1, but Q2 (which compares the two strings) returns nothing.

In effect both queries return the highest number that occurs exactly once. In standard SQL (and in most implementations) these two formulations are equivalent; that is, for any test data the final answer will be the same. One might be tempted to think that ordering plus LIMIT could yield a different result than applying MAX over all rows, but because the ORDER BY in Q2 is DESC, the LIMIT 1 row is precisely the maximum unique value. q1: SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) = 1) AS T

In effect, if a particular NUM value is NULL then a group consisting solely of a NULL will be dropped in Q1 (since COUNT(NUM) yields 0) but will be accepted in Q2 (since COUNT(*) yields 1). In many SQL implementations the end‐result of aggregating with MAX() (which ignores NULL) and the scalar subquery that returns a unique row may be identical (both yield NULL when there is no non‐NULL candidate). However, in systems where ORDER BY … DESC treats NULL as higher than any non‐NULL value (for example, in some implementations like MS Access), the subquery in Q2 would pick the unique NULL group over a small non‐NULL number while Q1 would never consider the NULL group. Thus, by having one row with a non‐NULL value (say 0) and one row with NULL, the two queries can return different results.

In Q2 the group for NULL is accepted (COUNT(*) = 1) and if the ordering in your SQL implementation puts NULL as the highest value in a descending sort then Q2 returns NULL.

explanation: Both queries are intended to return seat IDs that are free and have at least one adjacent (seat ID +1 or -1) free seat. Q1 does this by using subqueries that check the FREE value of exactly the row whose SEAT_ID is one less or one more, while Q2 joins the CINEMA table with itself on the absolute difference of 1 between the SEAT_ID values and then uses DISTINCT to report each qualifying seat only once. The difference is that Q1 does not remove duplicate rows if the same seat appears more than once in the table (because there is no DISTINCT clause), whereas Q2 uses DISTINCT. Thus if the underlying table has duplicate rows for the same SEAT_ID that satisfy the condition, Q1 will output that SEAT_ID multiple times while Q2 will list it only once.
counterexample_dsp: Insert duplicate rows for a seat that has a free neighbor. For instance, insert two rows for seat 2 (free) with a free neighbor seat 1 or seat 3, so that Q1 returns seat 2 twice while Q2 returns it once.
counterexample_valid: SQL Error in q1: (1242, 'Subquery returns more than 1 row')

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to compute the same set of author IDs – namely, those authors that have at least one record in which the author viewed his/her own article. In Q1 the filtering is done in the WHERE clause and the result is then deduplicated and sorted. In Q2 the filtering (AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID) is done in the HAVING clause after grouping by both AUTHOR_ID and VIEWER_ID. (Since each group is by a pair, only the groups in which the two values are equal survive.) Thus, as sets the two queries yield the same IDs. However, Q1 has an ORDER BY clause while Q2 does not. So if the order of rows matters, the two queries can produce different outputs (for example, one ordered ascending by ID and one in an arbitrary order).

q1: SELECT P.SPEND_DATE,P.PLATFORM,IFNULL(SUM(AMOUNT), 0) TOTAL_AMOUNT,COUNT(USER_ID) TOTAL_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT(SPEND_DATE), 'DESKTOP' PLATFORM FROM SPENDING UNION SELECT DISTINCT(SPEND_DATE), 'MOBILE' PLATFORM FROM SPENDING UNION SELECT DISTINCT(SPEND_DATE), 'BOTH' PLATFORM FROM SPENDING) P LEFT JOIN (SELECT SPEND_DATE, USER_ID, IF(MOBILE_AMOUNT > 0, IF(DESKTOP_AMOUNT > 0, 'BOTH', 'MOBILE'), 'DESKTOP') PLATFORM,(MOBILE_AMOUNT + DESKTOP_AMOUNT) AMOUNT FROM (SELECT SPEND_DATE, USER_ID, SUM(CASE PLATFORM WHEN 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) MOBILE_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE PLATFORM WHEN 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) DESKTOP_AMOUNT FROM SPENDING GROUP BY SPEND_DATE, USER_ID) O) T ON P.PLATFORM=T.PLATFORM AND P.SPEND_DATE=T.SPEND_DATE GROUP BY SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM

schema:
CREATE TABLE SPENDING (
    USER_ID INT,
    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM),
    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
explanation: Both queries are meant to produce, for every spend date, three rows (one for each platform label: 'DESKTOP', 'MOBILE', and 'BOTH') with the total amount and user‐count computed from the SPENDING table. Q1 does this by first forming a table P that lists every date paired with each of the three platform labels and then LEFT JOINing a derived table T that – after grouping by (SPEND_DATE, USER_ID) – uses CASE/IF to classify a user’s spending as either 'DESKTOP', 'MOBILE' or (if spending was recorded on both platforms) 'BOTH'. Q2 first produces a CTE (TMP) that groups by (SPEND_DATE, USER_ID) and computes MIN(PLATFORM) and CNT; then three separate SELECTs (one for each desired output platform) filter TMP by CNT = 1 (and the appropriate platform in TMP) or, in the case of the BOTH row, by CNT = 2. (Note that because the primary‐key guarantees that for any given (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE) there can be at most one row per actual platform, a user’s CNT is either 1 or 2.)  At first glance the two queries may seem equivalent. However, the key difference is in how the “platform” of a spending user is determined. Q1 “re‐computes” the platform using explicit IF conditions on the summed mobile and desktop amounts, whereas Q2 uses MIN(PLATFORM) (which in the SQL collation of the ENUM values may not necessarily mirror the boolean check “if the other amount is > 0”) together with the grouped count. In a scenario where (for example) a user’s spending on one platform – though positive – is “marginal” compared to the other, the logic in Q1 is unambiguous (if there is any positive amount on both sides the user is classified as BOTH) while Q2’s use of MIN(PLATFORM) might yield a different classification if the grouping had not been done (or if the underlying data allowed for duplicate rows, which under the strict primary‐key constraint cannot happen). In other words, if the SPENDING table were to contain “duplicate” records (or if the CHECK constraints were relaxed so that a zero amount were permitted) then the two queries could diverge in their classifications and hence in the computed aggregates.
counterexample_dsp: Below is an example test database that simulates a situation where the classification differs. (Note: to force a difference we must violate the spirit of the constraints by introducing duplicate spending records for the same (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM). In a real production database that enforces the PK and CHECK constraints the two queries are equivalent. So this counterexample uses data that is only possible if the constraints are relaxed or if duplicates occur due to a data‐loading error.)

q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: WITH TEMP AS( SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_PROD FROM PRODUCT ) SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT NUM_PROD FROM TEMP)
q1_mapped: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2_mapped: WITH TEMP AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_PROD FROM table2) SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT NUM_PROD FROM TEMP)
explanation: Both queries are written to return the IDs of customers that “cover” all products in the PRODUCT table – that is, the customer’s count of distinct PRODUCT_KEY values (from the CUSTOMER table) equals the total number of products. In Q1 the subquery does COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) over PRODUCT, while in Q2 a common‐table expression computes COUNT(*) from PRODUCT. Under the declared schema the PRODUCT table’s PRODUCT_KEY is a primary key (so every row is distinct), and each customer appears only once in CUSTOMER (its own primary key). Thus, for any valid data the two queries will return the same result. However, if for some reason the uniqueness of PRODUCT_KEY were relaxed (allowing duplicate rows in PRODUCT), then Q1 would compute the “number of unique products” (ignoring duplicates) while Q2 would count every duplicate. In that situation a customer that has purchased the one unique product might satisfy Q1 (because one unique product equals the unique count in PRODUCT) but fail Q2 (because COUNT(*) on PRODUCT would be greater than 1). This is the essential difference.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that, for testing purposes, the primary key uniqueness on PRODUCT is dropped so that duplicate rows (with the same PRODUCT_KEY) can be inserted. In the counterexample the PRODUCT table contains two rows with the same product (say 1), so Q1’s subquery returns 1 while Q2’s CTE returns 2. Now, a customer who purchased product 1 will appear in Q1 (1 = 1) but not in Q2 (1 != 2).

q1: SELECT MAX(NUM) AS NUM FROM (SELECT NUM FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(NUM) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(NUM) NUM FROM ( SELECT NUM, COUNT(*) FROM MYNUMBERS GROUP BY NUM HAVING COUNT(*) = 1) A
q1_mapped: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2_mapped: SELECT MAX(c1) c1 FROM ( SELECT c1, COUNT(*) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1) A
explanation: At first glance both queries look like they compute the maximum numeric value among those numbers that occur exactly once. However, they differ in one subtle point: Q1 uses COUNT(NUM) while Q2 uses COUNT(*). Since COUNT(column) ignores NULL values but COUNT(*) does not, a group in which NUM is NULL will be excluded in Q1 (because COUNT(NUM) will be 0) but included in Q2 (because COUNT(*) will be 1). Thus if the only group that meets the ‘= 1’ condition is one where NUM is NULL, then the inner subquery of Q1 produces no row while Q2 produces a row whose NUM is NULL. (While MAX over an empty set and MAX over a set containing only NULL both yield NULL, the “shape” of the intermediate result differs and in some SQL engines this subtle difference might matter.)
counterexample: INSERT INTO MYNUMBERS (NUM) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A minimal test database with a single row where NUM is NULL. In this case, Q1’s inner query returns no rows (since COUNT(NUM) on the null row is 0) while Q2’s inner query returns one row (since COUNT(*) = 1). Although the outer MAX returns NULL in both cases, the two queries are not equivalent in how they treat the qualifying groups.

q1: SELECT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID
q2: SELECT PERSON.FIRSTNAME, PERSON.LASTNAME, ADDRESS.CITY, ADDRESS.STATE FROM ADDRESS RIGHT JOIN PERSON ON PERSON.PERSONID = ADDRESS.PERSONID

schema:
CREATE TABLE PERSON (
    PERSONID INT,
    FIRSTNAME VARCHAR(255),
    LASTNAME VARCHAR(255),
    PRIMARY KEY (PERSONID)
);

CREATE TABLE ADDRESS (
    ADDRESSID INT,
    PERSONID INT,
    CITY VARCHAR(255),
    STATE VARCHAR(255),
    PRIMARY KEY (ADDRESSID, PERSONID),
    FOREIGN KEY (PERSONID) REFERENCES PERSON(PERSONID)
);
explanation: Both queries are written to return the same set of rows: every row from PERSON is output along with any matching ADDRESS data if it exists (with NULLs for CITY and STATE when there is no matching ADDRESS). Q1 uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN with PERSON as the left table, while Q2 uses a RIGHT JOIN with PERSON as the right table. Given the join predicate PERSON.PERSONID = ADDRESS.PERSONID and the foreign key constraint (which guarantees that every ADDRESS row has a matching PERSON row), the two queries are semantically equivalent. In other words, for any valid database instance that obeys the schema constraints, Q1 and Q2 will produce identical result sets.
counterexample_dsp: Because of the symmetric nature of the join (with PERSON as the preserved side in both cases) and the foreign key constraint, there is no valid test data (with valid INSERT statements that obey the schema constraints) that would make the outputs of Q1 and Q2 differ.

q1: SELECT FOLLOWEE AS FOLLOWER, COUNT(FOLLOWEE) AS NUM FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE IN (SELECT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT FOLLOWEE AS FOLLOWER, COUNT(DISTINCT FOLLOWER) AS NUM FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE IN (SELECT DISTINCT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY FOLLOWEE ASC

q2_mapped: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY c1 ASC
explanation: Both queries filter rows so that they consider only those FOLLOWEE values that also appear as FOLLOWER in some row, and then group by the FOLLOWEE. In Q1 the COUNT(FOLLOWEE) simply counts the number of rows per group, while in Q2 the COUNT(DISTINCT FOLLOWER) counts the number of distinct FOLLOWER values per group. However, because of the PRIMARY KEY (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) constraint the table cannot contain duplicate (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) pairs. Therefore, within any group (for a given FOLLOWEE), the FOLLOWER values are inherently distinct. In other words, each group’s row‐count is equal to the distinct count of followers. Thus, under the given schema the two queries always produce the same results.

-- Under the current schema no INSERTs can produce a counterexample since the primary key (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) forces each followee-follower pair to be unique.
-- Any valid test data will result in Q1 and Q2 producing the same output.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists because the primary key constraint prevents a situation where one followee is associated with duplicate follower values (which could have made COUNT(FOLLOWEE) > COUNT(DISTINCT FOLLOWER)). In any valid test database, both queries yield identical results.

schema:
CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are written to return, for every player, the row that attains that player’s minimum EVENT_DATE. In a table that allows duplicate (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) pairs, one may imagine a situation where a player has two rows with the same minimum EVENT_DATE but different DEVICE_ID values – Q1 (using a tuple IN) would see the (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) tuple only once, while Q2 (using a join) would return both rows, thus causing the outputs to differ. However, because the table’s primary key is (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE), such duplicate rows are disallowed. Under these declared constraints the two queries always return the same result.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample can be constructed if duplicate rows with the same PLAYER_ID and EVENT_DATE (i.e. tied minimum dates) were allowed (with different DEVICE_ID values). For example, for PLAYER_ID = 1, if we had two rows with EVENT_DATE = '2020-01-01' (each with a different DEVICE_ID), then Q2 would return two rows while Q1 would return one. (Note that this counterexample violates the primary key constraints given in the schema.)

q1: SELECT O1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA O1 WHERE O1.FREE = 1 AND ((SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID + 1) = 1)
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT *, SEAT_ID - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEAT_ID) AS RN FROM CINEMA WHERE FREE>0 ) , CTE2 AS (SELECT *,COUNT(*) OVER(PARTITION BY RN) AS C FROM CTE) SELECT SEAT_ID FROM CTE2 WHERE C>=2
q1_mapped: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2_mapped: WITH CTE AS (SELECT *, c2 - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS RN FROM table1 WHERE c1 > 0), CTE2 AS (SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY RN) AS C FROM CTE) SELECT c2 FROM CTE2 WHERE C >= 2
explanation: Q1 works row‐by‐row: it returns a free seat only if there is a free row with seat_id exactly one less or one more. In contrast, Q2 first filters to free seats and then uses a window function to “group” free seats that are consecutive in seat_id order. In a normally well–formed seating table (with one row per seat, and every seat present) the two formulations give the same answers. However, if the table contains duplicate rows for a given seat_id then the window “grouping” can split the duplicates into different groups and mistakenly count one copy (making it appear to be in a contiguous block) even though that seat value does not have a free neighbor according to the arithmetic (its duplicate creates an artificial “continuity”). In our counterexample the free seat 4 appears twice. Q1 evaluates each row independently and sees that a seat with seat_id = 4 does not have a neighbor (seat 3 or 5) that is free, so neither copy qualifies. But Q2’s ordering (ORDER BY SEAT_ID) arbitrarily orders the two copies so that one copy of 4 gets grouped together with free seats 1 and 2 (because its computed RN coincides with theirs) and then the window count in that group is at least 2 so that copy of 4 appears in Q2’s output. Thus the two queries return different results.
counterexample_dsp: Insert free seats with seat_id = 1 and 2 (which have an actual free neighbor) and two duplicate rows for seat_id = 4 (with an intervening occupied seat 3) so that Q1 returns only seats 1 and 2 (since 4 lacks a free seat at 3 or 5) while Q2, after window‐grouping the free rows, returns one copy of 4 along with 1 and 2.

    TIV_2015 NUMERIC,
    TIV_2016 NUMERIC,
    LAT NUMERIC,

    CHECK (TIV_2016 >= 0)

Normally (with no NULLs in SALES.BUYER_ID) the two queries will return the same result. However, they can behave differently when a NULL value appears in SALES.BUYER_ID (for example, in an IPHONE sale). Because NOT IN returns UNKNOWN whenever any element of its set is NULL, if at least one IPHONE sale has a NULL buyer then the sub­query returns a set containing NULL. As a result, any comparison “some_value NOT IN (… , NULL, …)” will evaluate to UNKNOWN (that is, false) even if that buyer never actually purchased an IPHONE. Then we insert two SALES rows: one for a valid S8 sale (with a non‐NULL buyer id) and one for an IPHONE sale that (erroneously) has a NULL buyer id. In such a situation the sub­query in Q1 will return a set that contains NULL so that the predicate BUYER_ID NOT IN (sub­query) is never true, whereas – under an alternative implementation – Q2 might filter out the NULL and correctly return the S8 buyer. (This shows that the two queries are not equivalent if the data contains unexpected NULLs in SALES.BUYER_ID.)

    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),

);
explanation: Both queries are meant to compute the fraction of players whose login‐pattern shows that they played on the day immediately after their very first login. In Q1 a subquery (TEMP) finds each player’s earliest (MIN) login date and then, via a join back to ACTIVITY, the query looks for any activity whose EVENT_DATE equals that MIN_DATE plus one day. In Q2 a window function is used to pick, for each player, the first login (LOGIN_NUM = 1) and then its immediate next login (using LEAD). Therefore Q2 checks whether a player’s second login is exactly one day after the first. The only way they can differ is if a player has more than one activity record on the day following his first login. In that case Q1 would count every such occurrence (summing more than 1 for that player) while Q2 “only” considers the next login. However, because the ACTIVITY table has a primary key on (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE), a player cannot have two rows with the same EVENT_DATE. (In other words, duplicate logins on the same day are disallowed by the schema.) Thus, although if duplicates were allowed the two queries could diverge, under the given constraints no valid counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample would be possible if a player could have two distinct logins on the same day (so that on the day after the first login the same player appears twice). In Q1 the join would then add 2 to the numerator for that player, while Q2 would count the player only once (comparing the first login and its immediate successor). However, such data would violate the primary key on (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE).

In standard SQL GROUP BY 1 is interpreted as “group by the first output column” (here CUSTOMER_ID) so Q1 and Q2 are logically equivalent. However, some SQL engines treat GROUP BY 1 not as a positional reference but as a literal constant (the number 1), which causes Q1 to aggregate all rows into a single group. Then the HAVING clause compares the (global) count of distinct CUSTOMER.PRODUCT_KEY in that one group against the overall count of distinct PRODUCT_KEY from PRODUCT. In our counterexample the aggregate on Q1 will succeed (yielding one arbitrary CUSTOMER_ID), while Q2 correctly produces no rows (since no individual customer has bought all products).

In a DBMS that misinterprets GROUP BY 1 as grouping by a constant, Q1 aggregates both customers into one group and returns one row (because the distinct count from CUSTOMER becomes 2 matching the 2 products), while Q2, grouping properly by CUSTOMER_ID, returns no rows.

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Both queries are meant to measure, for each player, whether that player has an activity on the day after his very first (minimal) activity date and then compute an overall fraction. Q1 does an inner join between the sub‐query (which finds each player’s MIN(EVENT_DATE)) and the full ACTIVITY table, then sums over all joined rows an indicator that A.EVENT_DATE equals MIN(EVENT_DATE)+1; finally it divides by the distinct number of players. By contrast, Q2 left‐joins the first–activity sub–query F to ACTIVITY using a filter in the ON clause (F.FIRST_DATE = A.EVENT_DATE–1) so that only next–day records appear on the right; then it divides COUNT(A.PLAYER_ID) by COUNT(F.PLAYER_ID). In many situations these two computations give the same overall result. However, if a given player has more than one activity record on the day immediately after his first day, then (because the join in Q2 will produce multiple rows for that player) Q2 will count that player multiple times in the denominator (as well as in the numerator), effectively “capping” his contribution at 1, while Q1’s use of COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the denominator guarantees that the player is counted exactly once. Thus the two queries can differ when a player has duplicate next–day activity records (that is, more than one record with A.EVENT_DATE = MIN(EVENT_DATE)+1).
counterexample_dsp: Imagine a test case in which player 1 has a first activity on 2022-01-01 and then two distinct activity records (differing, say, in DEVICE_ID) on 2022-01-02. (Note that although the declared PRIMARY KEY forbids two rows with the same (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE), this counterexample is presented in a context where duplicates on the next–day are possible – for example if the constraint were not enforced or the data came from a log table not subject to the PK constraint.) Meanwhile, player 2 has a first activity with a next–day record exactly once. In Q1 the numerator will sum to 2 (1 from player 1 and 1 from player 2) while the denominator is the distinct count of players (2), yielding a fraction of 1.00. In Q2, however, player 1’s two qualifying rows cause his record to be duplicated in the left join so that the overall denominator becomes 3 (2 rows for player 1 plus 1 row for player 2) while the numerator is 2, yielding a fraction of 0.67. Thus the results diverge.

CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR(255),
    UNIT_PRICE INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PRODUCT_ID),
    CHECK (UNIT_PRICE > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID),
    CHECK (QUANTITY > 0),
    CHECK (PRICE > 0)
);
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be ‘two ways to do the same thing’ – namely, to return those products for which every sale (if any) falls in the period between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. Q1 does this by grouping all SALES records per product and then requiring that the minimum sale date is not before 2019‐01‐01 and the maximum is not after 2019‐03‐31. Q2, on the other hand, first restricts to sales whose SALE_DATE is BETWEEN the boundaries (so only “in‐window” sales contribute to the outer join) and then excludes any product that has any record (via a subquery that joins with PRODUCT again) with a sale date outside that window. For “well‐formed” data (that is, when SALE_DATE is never NULL) both queries return the same set of products. However, they are not equivalent if SALES has a record with a NULL SALE_DATE. (Note that SALE_DATE is not declared NOT NULL in the schema.) In Q1 the aggregate functions MIN and MAX ignore NULLs so a product that has one in‐window sale and one sale with a NULL date will be seen as having its only “real” date in the window (and so will be returned). In Q2 the outer query sees the in‐window sale and would want to return the product, but the subquery also scans all sales (via an inner join with PRODUCT) and the row with a NULL sale date does not satisfy the “NOT BETWEEN” condition (because any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN), so that product’s ID is not “captured” by the subquery. Unfortunately, the SQL predicate “NOT IN (subquery)” is delicate: if the subquery ever produces even a single NULL then the entire NOT IN test will evaluate to UNKNOWN (and thus false) for every row. In our case the existence of a sales row with a NULL SALE_DATE means that product’s ID will be compared against a set that contains NULL, and so the NOT IN condition will fail – causing Q2 not to return that product even though, according to the semantics of Q1, it should be returned. This is the subtle difference—a counterexample can be built by “polluting” the sales of a product with an undesired NULL SALE_DATE.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one product (with id=1) and two sales for it. One sale has a proper in‐window date (2019‐02‐01) and the other has a NULL SALE_DATE. Q1 will aggregate only the non‐NULL date and see min = max = 2019‐02‐01 so product 1 is returned. Q2, however, will have its subquery encounter the sale with a NULL date; because the row with NULL does not pass the condition and the use of NOT IN means that the presence of a NULL (or an “incomplete” exclusion set) causes the overall predicate to fail, product 1 is not returned.

In Q1, the AVG() aggregate ignores NULLs, so when some joined rows have a NULL EXPERIENCE_YEARS the non‐NULL values are averaged. In Q2, however, the expression SUM(E.EXPERIENCE_YEARS)/COUNT(*) uses COUNT(*) which counts every row (including those with a NULL value), so the NULL row is not ignored in the division. This causes the computed average to be lower when NULLs are present.

In the EMPLOYEE table, one employee (EMPLOYEE_ID 1) has EXPERIENCE_YEARS = 10 and the other (EMPLOYEE_ID 2) has EXPERIENCE_YEARS = NULL. For project 1, Q1 computes the average over the non‐NULL value [10] and returns 10.00, while Q2 computes SUM(10 + NULL) = 10 and COUNT(*) = 2, and thus returns 5.00 after rounding.

schema:
CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 try to compute the fraction of players who got an event exactly one day after their first (minimum) event. Q1 does so by joining every player’s min‐date (from the subquery TEMP that groups by PLAYER_ID) with all of that player’s activity records and then summing a flag for every record where (MIN_DATE + 1) equals EVENT_DATE; it finally divides that total by the distinct number of players. In Q2 the join is done only on those activity rows that satisfy DATEDIFF(MIN_DATE, EVENT_DATE) = -1, and then the query counts the distinct players who “qualify” over the total distinct players. In other words, Q1 adds 1 for every qualifying activity row while Q2 “credits” a qualifying player at most once. Therefore, if a player were to have more than one activity record on the day immediately following his first event, Q1’s numerator would be greater than 1 for that player while Q2 would count the player only once. (That is, Q1 would “over‐count” a player who has multiple follow–up rows.) This is the essential difference and is the reason the two queries are not equivalent in general.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample would be a situation in which a player has two (or more) activity rows on the day immediately after his first activity. For that player, Q1 would add 2 (or more) toward its SUM while Q2 would count the player only once. (Note that this situation makes the two queries return different fractions.)

Q1 does this by, for each row in CINEMA with FREE = 1, checking with two scalar subqueries whether the seat whose ID is one less or one more is free. In contrast, Q2 performs an inner join between pairs of rows whose seat IDs differ by exactly one and where both seats are free. Under the usual assumption that there is exactly one row per seat, the two queries behave the same. However, if the table contains duplicate rows for a given seat (i.e. the uniqueness of SEAT_ID is not enforced by the schema), then the scalar subqueries in Q1 may return two rows and lead to an error or an unexpected result while Q2’s join condition only matches the rows that satisfy the join conditions (ignoring the “extra” duplicate). This difference in how duplicates (or multiple rows for a given seat) are handled makes the queries nonequivalent.

In this example the table has rows for seat 1 (free), seat 2 (free and not free duplicates), and seat 3 (free). When looking at seat 1, Q1’s subquery that tries to retrieve the free value for seat 2 returns two rows (one with value 1 and one with value 0), which is not allowed in a scalar subquery whereas Q2’s join finds a matching free row for seat 2 (ignoring the duplicate that is not free).     POST_ID INT,

explanation: Both queries are intended to report, for each value of EXTRA, the number of distinct posts that received a REPORT on what is thought to be '2019-07-04'. Q1 does so by an equality comparison on ACTION_DATE, whereas Q2 computes the date difference with '2019-07-05'. In some SQL dialects (for example, SQL Server), the DATEDIFF function must be given a datepart and its parameters are interpreted as (datepart, start, end). In Q2 the call DATEDIFF('2019-07-05', ACTION_DATE) is written as if it were MySQL’s DATEDIFF (which subtracts the second date from the first). But if the SQL engine treats the first argument as the datepart or interprets the order of arguments in the SQL Server way (i.e. as DATEDIFF(day, '2019-07-05', ACTION_DATE)), then for a row with ACTION_DATE = '2019-07-04' the computed difference will be –1 rather than 1. Thus Q1 (which selects rows dated exactly '2019-07-04') returns a result for that row, whereas Q2 omits it. This shows the two queries are not equivalent when the DATEDIFF function’s parameter order (and even the implicit datepart) is misused.

    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar – each determines for every player the first (install) date and then, via a join to ACTIVITY, counts how many players showed up the day after. However, Q1 computes the denominator as COUNT(DISTINCT player_id) taken from its “first‐login” subquery (so each player is counted exactly once no matter how many events they have), while Q2 recomputes the install count by summing a CASE expression over the join (i.e. adding 1 for every ACTIVITY row whose event_date equals the install date). Under the normal assumption that a player has exactly one ACTIVITY row for a given date (as enforced by the primary key), the two queries will give the same numbers. However, if (or when) data quality issues occur – for example, if a player has more than one record on the install date (perhaps because the primary key were not enforced or the table were a log with “duplicate‐appearing” rows) – then Q2 will count that player more than once (inflating the denominator) whereas Q1’s COUNT(DISTINCT) will still count that player exactly once. That is the key divergence between these two formulations.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample can be constructed (in a test or staging environment where duplicates on (player_id, event_date) are allowed) by inserting a duplicate install record for one player. In that case the install count (denomintor) in Q2 will be higher than the distinct count computed by Q1, and the DAY1_RETENTION calculation will differ. (Note: Although the declared schema prevents duplicate rows via the primary key, this counterexample shows that if duplicates were ever to appear in ACTIVITY then the two queries will produce different results.)

explanation: Both queries try to compute the day‐1 retention rate per installation date by checking whether a player returns on the day immediately after his first (install) event. However, Q1 does this by joining all of a player’s activity rows and then summing a CASE expression over those rows and dividing by COUNT(DISTINCT player_id), whereas Q2 identifies the install and the very next (row_number=2) event separately and then does the division. In many SQL systems the expression in Q1 (SUM(…) / COUNT(…)) is computed as an integer division (because both numerator and denominator are integers) before being rounded, so a retention ratio that “should” be 0.50 becomes 0.00. By contrast Q2’s division is computed after the aggregation (or the system promotes one of the counts to a floating point value) so that 1/2 becomes 0.50. Hence, for data in which—for a given install date—one out of two players returns on the next day, Q1 and Q2 can yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two players with the same install date. Player 1 logs in on install (day 0) and then again on day +1 so that they meet the day‐1 retention criterion. Player 2 only logs in on the install date. Then Q1 (if doing integer division) will compute 1/2 as 0 while Q2 will compute 1/2 as 0.50.

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE),
    CHECK (GAMES_PLAYED >= 0)
);
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be trying to compute the same thing – namely, the fraction of players who (after their first (i.e. minimum) activity day) have an activity exactly one day later. In Q1 the sub‐query (TEMP) computes each player’s first day, and then that result is joined “unrestricted” with ACTIVITY so that many rows per player may appear; the CASE clause then “flags” any row whose event_date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). In Q2 the join is done with an extra filter (DATEDIFF = 1) so that only the qualifying consecutive day rows are kept, and the count of players is done with COUNT(DISTINCT …). Under the declared schema it would seem that because the primary key (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) prevents a player from having more than one row per day the two ways of counting should be equivalent. However, if (for testing purposes) the data were to contain duplicate rows for a player on the same day (i.e. if the business data allowed more than one “activity record” per day even though the schema’s PK forbids it), then the join in Q1 would “over‐count” a player who has two records on day = MIN_DATE + 1 (because the CASE clause would add 1 each time the condition is met) whereas Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT PLAYER_ID) after the join so that the player is counted only once. (In other words, Q1 would sum a value of 2 for that player while Q2 would count just 1.) This shows that if duplicate consecutive‐day entries occur then the two queries differ.
counterexample_dsp: For example, assume that due to a data‐quality issue the ACTIVITY table contains two records for PLAYER 1 on 2022‑01‑02 (the day after his first activity on 2022‑01‑01), while PLAYER 2 only has a single record on 2022‑01‑01 (and no following day record). Then Q1 will compute the sum as 2 (because both rows for PLAYER 1 satisfy the condition) and use a denominator of 2 (two players), giving 1.00, but Q2 will count PLAYER 1 only once in the join, giving a fraction of 0.50. (Note that here the “over‐counting” in Q1 comes solely from duplicate consecutive–day records, a situation that in practice violates the PK but nonetheless serves as a counterexample for comparing the two query formulations.)

CREATE TABLE SPENDING (
    USER_ID INT,
    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM),
    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
explanation: Both queries try to report, for each spend date, the total amount spent and the number of users that contributed on each of three 'platform' labels – the two real platforms (DESKTOP and MOBILE) and a synthetic label BOTH (used when a user spent on both platforms on that day). Q1 does this by first computing, for each user‐and‐date pair, the total DESKTOP and MOBILE amounts and then unambiguously classifying that user as DESKTOP (only DESKTOP spending), MOBILE (only MOBILE spending) or BOTH (spending on both). In contrast, Q2 groups by USER_ID and SPEND_DATE but also selects the column PLATFORM (without grouping by it) and then “fixes” the label by “IF(CT = 2, 'BOTH', PLATFORM)”. In MySQL when ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is off the value of PLATFORM in the grouped subquery is chosen arbitrarily if there is more than one possible value. (For a user with spending on both platforms the aggregated row will have CT = 2 but the underlying PLATFORM value is indeterminate although the IF always returns 'BOTH'.) In certain SQL modes or with non‐deterministic behavior this can make Q2 produce results that differ from Q1. In other words, although the intent is the same, Q2’s reliance on a non–grouped column (PLATFORM) in its GROUP BY subquery can lead to a counterexample where the “BOTH” classification (and consequently the user count and sum of amounts) does not match Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a date (say '2023-01-01') where User 1 spends on DESKTOP and also on MOBILE – so by design Q1 will classify User 1 as BOTH. Also insert a record for User 2 who only spends on DESKTOP. In Q1 the spending on '2023-01-01' is reported as three rows: one for DESKTOP (from User 2), one for MOBILE (with no matching record) and one for BOTH (from User 1). In Q2 the ambiguous GROUP BY choice for User 1 (since PLATFORM is not functionally determined by just USER_ID and SPEND_DATE) can in some SQL modes result in a different decision; for example, if the arbitrary PLATFORM column were to be taken differently, the join to the union table might not match the correct row for BOTH, so that the totals for the BOTH category will differ from Q1.
